So the fundamental reason deceit is illegitimate is not the harm it does to the enemy. It is that it turns your own interior into the very structure you set out to oppose. Every use of it suppresses your own subjectivity once more and interrupts your own cultivation once more.

The European alliance system before 1914 shows this layer plainly. A web of secret treaties and military conventions ran between the great powers — obligations to enter a war, mobilization timetables, promises of support — and a substantial part of it was not disclosed to national parliaments or populations. Tens of millions of people were bound to commitments whose contents they did not know. When the crisis came and the timetables began to run, many learned what position they were standing in only after there was no way back.
That system could only function on the condition that its own citizens did not know. That is deceit.
5. Deceit in Four Positions
Run deceit through four different structural positions and its nature comes into focus.

Between two expansionist systems. Both can use deceit, and both do. Both also pay the price of having their own cultivation interrupted. This is what most historical wars look like — both sides lying to their own people, both structurally damaged, neither having climbed anywhere.

Between two subjects who genuinely recognize persons as ends. Deceit is neither usable nor useful. Their collisions take the form of disputation, and disputation requires mutual disclosure. A party that conceals from its own people does not even fully possess its own position, and cannot participate in disputation at all.
The defending, resisting side. This is the most important position: it cannot use deceit — not by choice, but because its structure will not let deceit start.

The next essay establishes a theorem: a warring party cannot not accept questioning. Deceit requires suppressing internal questioning. The two cannot coexist. The defender's soldiers, citizens, and dissenters can question decisions, and the commander cannot shut those questions down — because the moment he does, he has already fallen out of the position he occupies.

There is a deeper layer. The defender's structural goal is not to destroy the other side but to let the other side stand up as subjects. The suppressing party suppresses precisely because it has been instrumentalized by its own systemic purpose — the people inside it are suppressed subjects too. The defender's real work is to give those people a chance to come out of that instrumentalization. And that work cannot be done through deceit: deceit presupposes the other as an object that can be fooled, while liberation presupposes the other as a subject who can stand again. The two presuppositions exclude each other.

The suppressing side. The principal user of deceit, and its native ground. Systematic expansion structurally depends on deception running in two directions: inward, so the instrumentalized do not see the whole picture; outward, so the suppressed and third parties misread what it is.
But the bill deceit runs up against its own user is equally real, and it comes in three parts.
First, internal cultivation is broken outright. People held for long periods in deception and suppression are people in whom cultivation cannot occur.

Second, a short life. Maintenance costs rise monotonically until they exceed the returns from expansion, and the system collapses in its own internal contradictions. Large conquest structures frequently decay or fracture within a few generations. That is not a coincidence.

Third, and most interesting. Its soldiers and citizens notice that the other side does not use deceit, that the other side permits internal questioning, that the other side's operation is transparent. And a thought surfaces: why don't they do this on their side? Are we actually the side that is right?

That self-doubt accumulates slowly inside the suppressing party. And the self-doubt is itself cultivation's deepest work. A person who recognizes from the inside that deceit is the mark of a structural disadvantage is recognizing that he needs to come out of his own instrumentalization.
So deceit is not a long-term advantage for the suppressing side. It is that side's chronic self-destruction.
6. Deceit Locks Down the Whole Sequence
One last observation, and it is harder than everything above.
Deceit is not merely a structural problem at the level of arms. It locks down the entire upward sequence.
A subject in the habit of concealing from its own people cannot reach any level above.

Not disputation, because disputation requires honesty — including honesty inward. Not self-thought, because that requires moving the eyes off the opponent and back onto oneself, while deceit trains exactly the opposite reflex: stay fixed on the opponent while hiding from your own. Not non-attack, because that requires recognizing a field and leaving it, while deceit habituates you to staying in the field and operating. Not no-arms, because that requires standing inside persons-as-ends — including your own people as ends — while deceit stands inside "our own people may be used as instruments."

So the real consequence of "war is the way of deception," under these standards, is this: it compresses the entire possible space of collision-handling from a five-level spectrum down to the lowest rung.

That is the deepest reason to refuse deceit. Not that it fails to work — as a technique it is genuinely effective, at least in the short run. It is that deceit locks a civilization into the lowest level of arms and closes every channel upward.
7. The Credit Sunzi Is Owed
None of this is a moral evaluation of Sunzi. It is a structural observation. And he is owed full acknowledgment here.
That Sunzi could separate strategy from deceit twenty-three centuries ago is itself movement in the direction of persons-as-ends.

His hierarchy — attack strategy, then alliances, then troops, and last of all walled cities — means that arms are not all one thing. There are higher and lower levels, better and worse techniques, and different structural positions within arms. Steering a collision toward strategy is worth more than steering it toward a siege. Drawing that distinction at all is a form of structural self-awareness: it shows Sunzi already felt that "arms" is not a homogeneous toolbox but a field with internal levels.

Likewise, when he wrote that war is the way of deception, he did not glamorize deceit or promote it as war's highest form. On the contrary, within his own hierarchy, attacking strategy stands above attacking troops, and strategy stands above deceit. In the language available to him, he was already saying that attacking strategy is better than deceit.

Getting that far from where he stood is remarkably deep. It means Sunzi already sensed that not all techniques of war are equivalent, that some are more worth pursuing than others, and that the highest technique is the one that does not require fighting. In this framework's language those intuitions would be called orientation toward mutual recognition, toward preserving cultivation, toward climbing the sequence — but none of that vocabulary existed for him. He used what he had, and pushed it as far as it would go.

He saw the difference between strategy and deceit. All this series can do is state the structural reason for that difference: strategy does not suppress subjects, deceit does; open play lets the other participate as a lucid subject, deceit uses one's own as instruments; strategy's force comes from a real contest of intelligence, deceit's from an information gap; time stands with strategy and open play, and stands against deceit.

Sunzi could not have said those reasons. He felt them. Someone who could feel that twenty-three centuries ago was holding cultivation's direction open at his own level. That we can now state it in a later vocabulary is standing on his shoulders — and that continuity is itself one of the ways cultivation happens.
Next
The locating work is done, and so is the technical taxonomy. What comes next is the hardest part of this series: four constraints.
All four begin with the same words — cannot not.
head_title_parts: Strategy, Scheme, Open Play, and Deceit

en/ep05.title: Essay 5: Four Cannot-Nots
en/ep05.deck: Cannot not start, cannot not expand, cannot not be directed toward ending, cannot not be open to questioning. Four concentric constraints, penetrating from the initiation of an act down to the very form in which a warring party exists as a subject.
units: The first four essays were all locating work: what war is, where it sits, how it relates to the structures around it, what divisions run inside it. Only once that is done can standards be set.
This essay is the hardest part of the series — four theorems constraining war. Together they form cultivation's complete protective mechanism inside a wartime situation.
1. The Shared Grammar
Here are all four side by side.

Theorem One · Cannot not start. Beginning a war must satisfy a cannot-not: every route through negotiation and maneuver has been exhausted, subjectivity has been forced to its limit, and without fighting, cultivation will be entirely broken in this field.
Theorem Two · Cannot not expand. Once a war has begun, every expansion must pass a fresh test at the level of Theorem One. "We are already fighting" may not be used to smuggle anything through.

Theorem Three · Cannot not be directed toward ending. Every action in a war must point toward its ending — the moment the original cannot-not is dissolved and cultivation regains the conditions to continue.

Theorem Four · Cannot not be open to questioning. A warring party holds no privilege of going unquestioned. The questioning may come from its own interior, from inside the other side, from third parties, or from future history.
All four begin with the same words: cannot not.
This is not stylistic symmetry. "Cannot not" performs a specific structural function — it strips the subject of its sense of power.

The typical grammar for handling war is "I decide," "I permit," "I judge," "I have the right." That grammar puts the warring party in the position of sovereign: he chooses how to fight, when to stop, whether to accept questioning.

"Cannot not" cancels that position. It says: the party is not choosing to go to war, it has been forced into a corner by structure and cannot not go. It is not permitting questioning; it has no position available from which to go unquestioned.

This grammatical discipline is not a preference. It is the shell the principle lives in. Grant the warring party the grammatical standing of a permitter, and you have structurally opened the door to the Kingdom of Means.
2. Theorem One · Cannot Not Start
The beginning of a war is a threshold. Cross it, and cultivation undergoes extreme-state handling. So the threshold has to be set very high.
The test has two conditions, and both must hold at once.

External condition: routes through negotiation and maneuver are exhausted. Contests at the level of wisdom, bargaining over interests, diplomacy, third-party mediation, the making and repairing of agreements — every non-violent route has been tried and has failed. Not abandoned after one or two attempts, but genuinely exhausted: under the existing structure there is no non-violent path left.

Internal condition: subjectivity has been forced to its limit. One's own position as a subject has reached the point where it will be lost without resistance — the carrier of cultivation itself is about to be eliminated. Note what this does not mean: not injured interests, not wounded pride, not possible future insecurity. It means that existence as a subject can no longer be structurally sustained.

Neither condition suffices alone. Meet only the first, and cultivation can still continue by other means — endurance, concession, trading time for space. Meet only the second, and there are still non-war routes untried.
Under this test, the following common reasons for starting a war all fail.
Preventive war (they may threaten us later, so strike first) — a future threat has not caused present loss of one's own cultivation.
Demonstrative war (fight one to warn the others) — this uses the other side's soldiers as carriers of a signal, which structurally instrumentalizes them already.

War for gain (resources, territory, trade rights) — acquiring gains is not defending cultivation. Applying the vocabulary of protecting cultivation to a contest over spoils is the most typical slide of all.
War for honor (an insult, an affront) — damaged honor does not touch cultivation's continued existence.

Pre-emption — this requires strict separation. If the other side's attack is genuinely underway, that is not pre-emption, it is resistance. If it is merely about to happen, we are back at preventive war.
3. Seeing Is Not Substituting
Theorem One contains a structure that is easy to misread, and it needs unpacking on its own.

"Defending subjectivity" has two faces. The first is defending one's own, and that is the trunk. The second is recognizing suppressed subjectivity inside the other side — sometimes the situation is not only that we are being pressed, but that people inside the other side have been pressed to the limit too.
Can the second face alone justify starting a war?
No. It can only be something seen alongside a first face that already holds.
And four extremely strict gates apply.

Gate one: it cannot start anything by itself. A subject may not cross a border to make war because "another country oppresses some of its people." Doing so treats war as an instrument for solving someone else's problem on their behalf, and that substitution is itself another cancellation of the suppressed party's subjectivity. Time after time in history, wars of liberation and humanitarian interventions have begun their slide at exactly this gate.

Gate two: seeing is not substituting. Even where the first face holds, recognition of the suppressed inside the other side must remain a posture of seeing. I can acknowledge your predicament and that you should be released as a subject; I do not decide what you are to become, choose your leaders, or plan your future.

Gate three: the rising must be real. The suppressed party's rising must be a genuine self-declaration from inside, not an appearance manufactured from outside, not a resistance that exists only because outside support keeps it alive, not something constructed to supply legitimacy for someone else's war. Outsiders may recognize and may support. They may not manufacture.

Gate four: an intervening party should have stakes of its own. This is the most counterintuitive: a completely "selfless" cross-border intervention is structurally suspect — a selfless intervention has no cannot-not of its own, and therefore no position at which it can be held accountable. A party with a genuinely legitimate position to intervene usually has stakes in the collision itself. Stakes are not a stain. They are a healthy anchor.

But "stakes" must be defined precisely. Not expansionist interest — territory, resources, markets — but the intervening party's own cultivation already being caught up in the situation. And a harder limit applies: that involvement must be structural erosion happening right now, not a future risk inferred from a forecast.

This boundary matters enormously, because "future risk" is the seedbed of every preventive-war rhetoric: they will threaten us eventually; if we do not fight them, we will be affected too; once they are strong it will be too late. That rhetoric can package any expansion as defense.
The line falls here: a party genuinely protecting its own cultivation can point at what is already happening. A party pretending to protect its cultivation can only point at a prediction.
4. Theorem Two · Cannot Not Expand
A war has begun. That is only the first structural judgment. War is not static — it shifts, spreads, escalates. And no shift automatically inherits the legitimacy of what came before it.

Expansion is not one-dimensional. Expansion of scope (from a local theater to a wider geography), of intensity (from limited engagement to total war), of participants (bringing in allies, drawing in third parties), of objective, of duration, of means — an expansion along any one of these axes must pass its own separate test.
The test has this form: without expanding, the position defended under Theorem One will be lost.

An adequate expansion has to satisfy three things at once. The position originally defended is in fact being lost. The direction of expansion still points directly at dissolving the original cannot-not. And the search for non-war routes has not stopped just because fighting has started — before expanding, one must confirm those routes remain closed.
There is a particular trap to watch for here: the drift of a war's objective while it runs.

Three drifts are most common. From defending to destroying — what began as keeping subjectivity from being lost becomes destroying the other as a subject. From removing a threat to remaking the other — what began as stopping suppression becomes turning the other into the "correct" shape. From resolving the present conflict to settling it once and for all — what began as handling this cannot-not becomes eliminating every possible future threat.
None of these constitutes a legitimate expansion. They are the objective going out of bounds — even when they look more thorough, more efficient, more decisive in military terms.

The Napoleonic wars are the long case study in objective drift. The starting point was structurally defensible: a young republic facing coordinated intervention by several dynasties is a real defensive situation. But over the following decade and more the objective slid steadily outward — from repelling intervention, to installing sister republics in neighboring states, to redrawing the map of Europe, to distributing relatives as kings, and finally to marching into a great power in 1812 to force compliance with a trade blockade.
Each step grew "naturally" out of the last. And not one step turned back to ask: is the cannot-not that justified starting still there?

Something else moved in step with it. Conscription levels, censorship, and the police apparatus inside France deepened with every expansion. External expansion and internal suppression were indeed two faces of one thing.
A war that began as defense spent more than a decade, without a single expansion test ever being applied, becoming the thing it had originally opposed.
5. Theorem Three · Cannot Not Be Directed Toward Ending
For a war legitimately started and legitimately expanded, the next structural question is whether it is running toward its own end.
"Ending" has a precise sense here. It does not mean the other side surrendering, being destroyed, or accepting our terms. Those states may accompany an ending, but they are not what the ending is.
The ending is the moment the original cannot-not is dissolved — the moment cultivation regains the conditions to continue.
This definition anchors the end of a war outside the war, rather than in any internal state of winning or losing. That anchoring is the key to the whole theorem.
From it follows a constraint that hangs directly beneath Theorem Three:
Constraint on means: any means that forecloses the possibility of that ending in advance, or that structurally makes the other side's post-war cultivation impossible, is inadequate in principle.

Not because such means are cruel or inhumane — those are ethical judgments, which this framework does not make. Because they structurally destroy the direction of cultivation's recovery. At the moment they are used, Theorem Three has already been violated.

Which means? Large-scale indiscriminate killing and injury, where it removes at a stroke the basis on which the other side could recover as a carrier of cultivation. Precision strikes aimed at the capacity for reconstitution — eliminating a cultural core, an educational core, a spiritual core in one blow. Even where casualty figures look modest, if the effect is that the other side cannot reorganize as a carrier of cultivation, the constraint is violated. And irreversible structural alteration — rendering a place uninhabitable long-term, destroying heritage that cannot be rebuilt.

Carthage in 146 BCE is the standard case on the wrong side of this line. When the war ended, the city was systematically demolished, the surviving population sold into slavery, and the land reorganized as a province. What was done went past removing an opponent's military capacity. It removed the minimum conditions under which a civilization could stand up again at all.

The result: that war did not end at the moment cultivation could continue again. It ended at the moment the other side ceased to exist as a carrier of cultivation. Those are two entirely different ending forms.
But the constraint needs a precise boundary, or it will be read too broadly.

It does not forbid every action that weakens the other side. Striking the other side's present capacity to suppress, its present war-making capacity, its present military organization — these may well be adequate, if they serve to dissolve the cannot-not.
The boundary falls here: present capacity to suppress may be struck; the minimum conditions for post-war reconstitution may not.

This boundary also imposes a retroactive requirement on the decision to start. At the moment a subject decides whether to begin, it must already be able to answer: if this war is fought, how does it end? How does cultivation continue on both sides afterward? What condition is the other side in when it is over?

An inability to answer means the sense of direction has not been established. And a war without a sense of direction will almost certainly lose direction while running — and what it breaks in the end is not only the other side's cultivation but its own.
6. Theorem Four · Cannot Not Be Open to Questioning
The first three theorems constrain what a war does. The fourth constrains what the warring party is.

It is also the deepest of the four, because it protects the warring party's own cultivation. The first three mainly prevent a war from breaking the other side's cultivation. The fourth prevents the warring party from breaking its own — through suppressed dissent, eliminated questioning, deified decision-makers.
A warring party that permits no questioning has already broken its own internal cultivation. Even winning militarily, it has lost the internal conditions for cultivation to continue afterward.
Theorem Four also holds a special position: it is simultaneously a norm and a diagnostic.

Judgments under the first three theorems can be self-declared. A party can say it has exhausted every route, that its expansion was necessary, that it is oriented toward ending. Those declarations are very hard to verify from outside, because outsiders cannot see the internal process of judgment.
Theorem Four is different. Whether questioning is permitted is directly visible from outside.
But seeing it accurately takes four layers of diagnosis.
Layer one: does questioning exist? Is anyone, any institution, any channel actually questioning? If everyone who dissents is removed and every channel is closed, Theorem Four fails immediately.
Layer two: can questioning reach the decision core? Questioning that circulates only at the periphery does not count. It has to reach the highest decision-makers and the core mechanism of decision.

Layer three: are questioners protected? Are they suppressed, persecuted, or sidelined for questioning? If the act itself carries a cost, then even where questioning still occurs, it is not sustainable.
Layer four: does questioning actually affect decisions? Even with the first three satisfied, if the results of questioning carry no weight in the decision, the questioning is theater.
All four layers must hold. One breach is failure.
The Athenian debate of 415 BCE over the Sicilian expedition is the best teaching case for these four layers — because the first three passed and the fourth failed.

Questioning existed: the assembly debated in the open, and both those urging the expedition and those opposing it spoke. It reached the decision core: the assembly was the decision, and nothing is more central than that. Questioners were protected: Nicias, who opposed the expedition publicly, was not punished for it — he was appointed one of its commanders.

Then the fourth layer broke. Hoping to talk the assembly out of the idea, Nicias described the forces and supplies such an expedition would require in the most extravagant terms, expecting the sheer scale to frighten everyone off. The assembly's response was to approve everything he had named and send a larger expedition.
The questioning was heard, recorded, even "adopted." It did not change the direction of the decision. It only changed its magnitude.
That is exactly why the case is valuable: having a debate is not the same as passing Theorem Four. The four layers have to be checked one by one.
One more point. Faking openness to questioning can succeed over short timescales and must fail over long ones.

In the short run, a warring party can manufacture the appearance of passing Theorem Four through information control, performative mechanisms, and quiet persecution of questioners. But genuine openness to questioning is an expression of the health of a society's subjectivity, and that health shows up directly, over long stretches, in the rate of development. A society that permits no real questioning has its internal subjects systematically suppressed; they contribute no genuine creativity or judgment; and its development rate necessarily falls behind — with the gap accumulating exponentially across decades and generations.
A short-run disguise can pass. Over long timescales, the bill is settled at the level of development.
7. The Four Are One Thing
Though all four share a grammar, "cannot not" constrains a different object in each, forming a sequence of increasing penetration.

Theorem One constrains the initiation of an action. Theorem Two constrains its continuation and escalation. Theorem Three constrains its direction. Theorem Four constrains the warring party's own position — it does not restrain any particular act; it restrains the form in which the party exists as a subject.

Initiation, continuation, direction, position. Theorem Four penetrates deepest: before it, the warring party loses the identity of permitter. He is not the one who permits questioning. He is the one who undergoes it.
So the four are not a flat checklist of norms. They are concentric constraints — each one protecting cultivation from being swallowed by war at a deeper level than the last.

One further observation: the four reinforce each other. A subject that starts adequately under Theorem One usually also tests expansions strictly, orients toward ending, and permits questioning — because all of these come from the same source. The reverse holds too: a subject violating one usually violates the others. Such violations are not independent events. They are multiple symptoms of a single structural tendency.

Which means that assessing whether a war meets the criteria usually does not require a complete judgment on all four. And Theorem Four, as the externally observable diagnostic, is especially useful — look at it, and you can usually infer the approximate state of the other three.
The four theorems are not norms for war. They are cultivation's protective mechanism inside a war.
Next
Wars end. And there are only three ending forms: victory, defeat, and a balance of power.
Each carries its own temptation. And the one that most needs to be refused outright is, in a good many civilizations, treated as the most dignified choice available.

en/ep06.title: Essay 6: Victory, Defeat, Balance of Power
en/ep06.deck: A victor's two obligations and the firewall against liberating on someone's behalf; why defeat is not losing and self-annihilation is never structurally adequate; and the most hidden toxicity in a balance of power, called mirror assimilation — you never lost on the battlefield, but across the standoff you became their mirror.
units: Wars end. And there are only three ending forms: victory, defeat, and a balance of power.

None of the three is chosen by the warring party. They are what the two sides' structural positions produce between them. What a party can choose is only this: inside the form it finds itself in, how to let cultivation actually return.
Each form carries its own temptation. And all three temptations point at the same thing — freezing some wartime state into a new long-term one, so that cultivation still cannot come back afterward.
1. Three Conditions for Victory
Victory under these standards has three necessary conditions, all of which must hold.

The cannot-not that justified starting has been dissolved by the war. At the same time, the other side still exists as a subject of cultivation. And the victor has not, in the process, become a new suppressive structure itself.

Fail the first while winning militarily, and this is not victory but a war whose work is unfinished. Fail the second — the other side destroyed, wholly remade, no longer existing as a subject — and this is not victory either, but an ending form that terminates the other's cultivation, however total it looks in military terms.

The third condition is the one most easily overlooked. If a defender builds itself into another suppression machine while resisting, then even winning is a net loss for cultivation as a whole: the world has one fewer defender and one more suppressor.
2. The Great Temptation After Victory

To fight a war, a victor has to build suppressive structures: centralized command, emergency powers, temporary limits on dissent, a society-wide mobilization apparatus. In wartime these may well be adequate.
After the war, their legitimacy vanishes in the same second — the war is over, the wartime reason is gone.

The structures themselves do not vanish with it. Command hierarchies do not dissolve on their own, emergency powers are not handed back automatically, mobilization machinery does not shut itself off. So the victor faces a choice: dismantle them deliberately, or let them continue as the peacetime structure of domination?

The moment continuation is chosen, the victor has turned itself into a new machine. What it presses on may be its own people, using the power built in wartime, or the defeated side's people, in the name of "managing the postwar situation."
This is the most common route by which a victor falls: the permanentization of wartime structure.
So a victor carries two explicit structural obligations.
First, dismantle wartime structures deliberately. The speed and thoroughness of that dismantling determine directly whether the victor is still standing where it started.

Second, withdraw from the space in which the defeated side reconstitutes its subjectivity. Winning does not confer the right to remake the loser. How the defeated side reorganizes its society, chooses its leaders, and recovers its subjectivity is the defeated side's own business. A victor that crosses the line from "removing the threat" into managing the other's internal affairs — even under the banners of reconstruction, aid, and preventing chaos — is exercising the other's choices on its behalf.
3. The Firewall Against Liberating on Someone's Behalf
The second obligation deserves its own treatment, because it answers the most deceptive temptation of the postwar period.

If the victor really was the suppressed party and the loser really was the suppressor, then winning has itself given the people suppressed inside the loser some opening toward release. And a thought arrives very easily at this point: since we have won, we ought to "help" them build a new society, a new order, new institutions.
On the surface this looks like goodwill. In substance it is liberation-by-proxy — the victor deciding, on the loser's behalf, what the loser should become.
The result is to move the liberated from one suppression to another. Their subjectivity has not actually been released; only the structure pressing on it has changed.

So the firewall reduces to one sentence: a victor may not decide the defeated side's direction of development for it. Not its ceiling of value, not its narrative, not the shape of its future. Once the threat is removed, reconstruction must be handed back quickly to real subjects inside the defeated society.

But a firewall is not the same as absolute non-interference — absolute non-interference is the error at the other pole. If, after the victor withdraws, a new suppressive structure immediately arises inside the defeated side and begins slaughtering its own people, must the victor hold to non-interference?
No. That constitutes a new situation, to be tested afresh under Theorem One rather than inheriting the previous war's authorization automatically.
So the firewall is correctly stated as: do not colonize, but keep watching.

Not colonizing holds the firewall. Watching keeps open the channel for a fresh test. The concrete form — whether to station forces, how many, for how long — belongs to executors. Philosophy supplies only the direction.
The two postwar settlements of 1815 and 1919 diverge visibly on exactly this boundary.

In 1815, the defeated state's representative was allowed a seat at the table, the defeated state was retained in the European system as a normal member, borders returned roughly to their prewar lines, and the occupation ended within a few years. What was dealt with was the expansionist structure that had been overthrown, not that country's existence as a subject.

In 1919, the defeated state took no part in the negotiations, and the treaty was delivered for signature in the form of an ultimatum. Article 231 required Germany to accept that Germany and its allies were responsible for the loss and damage caused to the Allied powers and their nationals by the war arising from their aggression. This reparations clause was also widely understood as a judgement of war guilt, becoming an important source of humiliation for the defeated party.

No causal claim is being made here. The origins of a war are always more complicated than any single treaty, and simply hanging what happened twenty years later on 1919 is dishonest history. The observation is structural only: on the question of whether the defeated side remains in the system as a subject, the two settlements ran in opposite directions. And that question is precisely the line the firewall draws.
4. Defeat: The Carrier Falls, Cultivation Does Not End
Defeat, under these standards, is defined as this: the concrete carrier of cultivation is lost, but cultivation itself has not ended.

Both halves matter. "The carrier is lost" is an objective fact — the main position is gone, the capital has fallen, the existing organization is dissolved, the former way of life cannot continue. "Cultivation has not ended" is something else — it can continue in exile, in dispersal, in memory, in the next generation.
So defeat is the failure of one concrete form of cultivation, not the disappearance of cultivation.
This yields a distinction of enormous importance to a defeated party: defeat is not losing.

A subject can fail completely in military terms while sustaining cultivation throughout — that subject has not lost. It has been defeated. A subject can win victory after victory while breaking its own cultivation — that subject has lost, whatever territory it holds.

The two axes are entirely separate. The concrete form of your defeat is often outside your control — relative force, outside help, contingency. Whether cultivation continues through your defeat lies inside your own judgment and action.
5. Against Self-Annihilation
Before the concrete responses available to a defeated party, this series' hardest claim has to be set down.

Nearly every other framework's war thought endorses collective self-annihilation in some situation — when defeat is irreversible and humiliation unacceptable, going down to the last is treated as the dignified choice. The Chinese phrase is "better a shattered jade than an intact tile," and versions of it recur across civilizations, always carrying tragedy, honor, and the dignity of at least not having yielded.
This series refuses that outright.
Self-annihilation is structurally inadequate. There is no situation in which it is an adequate form of defeat.

The reason is not a value claim about the preciousness of life. It is structural. This framework's axiom is that subjectivity cannot be eliminated and cultivation cannot not continue. The structure of self-annihilation is a subject actively choosing to make cultivation's carrier disappear — not a termination imposed from outside but one chosen from within. It collides with the axiom directly.

And once the carrier is gone, what is lost is not only that subject. The cultivation borne by a subject carries the history of its mutual sharpening with others, the memory of growing alongside them, the directions it might still have taken. The carrier's disappearance takes all of that with it. Cultivation requires mutual sharpening, and self-annihilation makes a possible future partner disappear permanently — even a present enemy may be a partner across a long enough span, and this severs that possibility.
There is a deeper layer still: the "total disappearance" that self-annihilation aims at does not structurally exist.

Suppressed subjectivity returns — in surviving descendants, in historical memory, in the inheritance carried by witnesses, in the language, culture, and traditions left behind. So at the very moment a subject believes it has completed its disappearance, its subjectivity has already begun returning in another form. And the intensity of that return is proportional to the finality of the act: the more absolute the annihilation, the deeper the trauma and memory left behind, and the stronger the return.
The cost of self-annihilation is real — a generation, or several, gone. The goal it aims at is false.

Numantia in 133 BCE is the specimen. Besieged on the Iberian peninsula until nothing was left, most of its inhabitants chose an end that kept them from being taken, and the city was afterward levelled.

What followed proves the impossibility of total disappearance. Numantia became a name retold for the next two thousand years; "Numantine resistance" turned into a fixed expression; Cervantes wrote a tragedy about it. It returned in the form of commemoration. It simply was not there to take part in its own return.
One especially dangerous situation has to be addressed here: the purist trap.

A subject in the middle of evolving from a suppressive structure toward persons-as-ends can regress under the extreme pressure of defeat. It repackages self-annihilation in the language of purity, dignity, and refusing to yield to barbarism. That packaging is particularly dangerous because it speaks in cultivation's own voice: our civilization is too precious to survive in humiliation.
The sentence sounds like a defense of cultivation. In substance it demands the disappearance of cultivation's carrier in cultivation's name.
When the carrier goes, cultivation breaks. There is no "purity" more important than the carrier's continuation.

A final observation: self-annihilation becomes a stable, visible option only when both sides are locked in the same vocabulary. The pressed side understands its situation in the language of honor and winning or losing, so going down looks dignified as the end approaches; the pressing side treats the other as an enemy rather than as a subject who has not yet stood up, so it drives the other into a corner and leaves no room for continuing as a subject. Only when the two vocabularies interlock does the option take shape.
A suppressing party genuinely operating on persons-as-ends — if that phrase still applies — actively prevents the situation from arising: what it wants is the other standing up, not the other gone.
So the appearance of self-annihilation is itself a diagnosis: in any war where it appears, at least one side is still on the lower level.
6. Three Adequate Responses
With that established, the positive question is what an adequate response looks like once defeat is certain.
It depends on what the other side wants. Three cases.

They want gains — trade gains for time. The mildest situation. They want resources, territory, trade rights, tax revenue, a posture of submission. They are not pursuing your disappearance as a subject.

The response is to concede at the level of gains while preserving your integrity as a subject of cultivation. The critical thing is knowing what may be conceded and what may not. Concedable: concrete interests, dignity for a time, nominal allegiance, some autonomy. Not concedable: the carrier itself — culture, language, spiritual tradition, education, the way subjectivity operates in daily life. Once those begin to be replaced, this is no longer trading gains for time. It is assimilation on an installment plan.
Time is cultivation's ally. Horace said what this road looks like when it works, in one line: captive Greece took her savage conqueror captive.

They want you gone as a subject, and you can still leave — leave. Not shameful flight, but the clear-eyed recognition that this concrete form cannot be sustained, and the deliberate deferral of it to a future in which it can be rebuilt.

Key people relocated, essential resources protected, the carriers of tradition — books, crafts, knowledge, transmission — moved somewhere safe first. This demands very clear judgment from leadership: choosing to withdraw while it still looks possible to make a stand often preserves far more than withdrawing from a corner. Those who leave early can take the core with them; those who leave at the end often bring out only a remnant.

The Huguenot emigration after 1685 demonstrates this at scale. When the edict of toleration was revoked, roughly two hundred thousand people left France over the following years for the Netherlands, Prussia, England, Switzerland, and further. They did not leave empty-handed — silk-weaving, clockmaking, printing, and finance travelled with the people who knew them. Decades later those crafts were flourishing where they arrived and declining where they had left.
Leaving means moving cultivation's carrier out of a field that is closing and into one that is still open.
They want you gone, and you cannot leave — disperse. The harshest situation. It runs in two directions.

Inward dispersal. The organization as a whole dissolves, but cultivation does not — it moves from the macroscopic and visible into the microscopic, individual, familial, and unseen. An occupier can destroy a government, a capital, an army. It has great difficulty destroying tens of millions of dispersed individuals. As long as cultivation continues at the level of persons and households, the occupation cannot complete itself.
Every person who keeps speaking their own language under occupation, every text passed secretly from hand to hand, every lesson taught in a private parlour, is cultivation in dispersed form.

Poland between 1795 and 1918 is the fullest demonstration. The country was erased from the map of Europe for one hundred and twenty-three years, partitioned among three neighbors, its language banned in schools and its history rewritten in textbooks. Cultivation moved into households, churches, private libraries, and clandestine classrooms. The Flying University, which appeared in 1885 — an underground institution with no fixed premises, changing location for each session to stay ahead of the police — taught several thousand students over the following decades. Marie Skłodowska was one of them.

A hundred and twenty-three years later the country reappeared on the map. What brought it back was not any single battle. It was the thing that had never stopped during those hundred and twenty-three years.

Outward connection. Dispersal is not only inward. It also means finding allies of the same structure — weaving your own cultivation into a network that spans subjects. One subject may fail; cultivation as a trans-subjective phenomenon remains.

Four points here. First, allies must be structurally alike — ally with another suppressive structure on the logic that an enemy's enemy is a friend, and sooner or later that ally will act like what it is and destroy with its own hands what you preserved. Second, an ally must protect your subjectivity rather than liberate on your behalf; the firewall above applies inside alliances too, and not all aid is adequate aid. Third, an ally having stakes of its own is a healthy anchor, not a stain. Fourth, outward connection is no cure-all: sometimes there is no ally to find, and dispersal can only go inward — at greater cost, over longer time, depending more heavily on internal resilience.

There is a grimmer grey zone: no structurally similar ally exists, and survival requires borrowing strength from another suppressive structure. This series does not pretend that situation never occurs, and does not offer a simple yes or no — because an absolute prohibition would, at that extremity, push a subject back toward self-annihilation. ("Better to vanish honorably than to borrow from the wicked" is just the purist trap in another accent.)

The only standard available here is this: if such shelter must be accepted, an internal firewall has to be held continuously — use the physical shelter, never internalize the purpose. The moment the firewall fails, dispersal has already become colonization by a new structure. Whether it can be held is a situational judgment, not something philosophy can answer in general.
7. Balance of Power and Mirror Assimilation
The third form is a balance of power: neither side can dissolve its own cannot-not by continuing to fight. Fighting on will not let either side's cultivation recover.
In that situation, Theorem Three's "directed toward ending" becomes something concrete: stop. Continuing no longer points toward cultivation's recovery; it only extends the interruption.

But stopping is only the first step. The second is returning to negotiation and maneuver — if the collisions that caused the war have not been handled, they will still be there, only now handled by other means.
Both steps are necessary. Stopping without returning to non-war routes is a different error: cultivation still cannot come back, it merely stops being interrupted by specific military actions.
The great danger here is turning a cessation into a truce.

Cessation is the stopping of military action. A real ending is the ending of the state of war — both sides return to a non-war relationship and cultivation can unfold between them again. A truce is the state in between: the guns are quiet, but the war has not ended, both sides still regard each other as enemies, preparation continues, and society still runs on wartime logic.
A truce looks like peace. In substance it makes the wartime state permanent.
And a long truce carries a hidden toxicity that deserves its own name: mirror assimilation.

The structure works like this. To guard against the other side over a long standoff, you must increasingly come to resemble it in organization, institutions, narrative, and mobilization. They have a powerful mobilization apparatus, so you build one to match. They use a wartime narrative to hold their interior together, so you use one too, to avoid being outdone. They suppress internal dissent to maintain unity, so you suppress yours to avoid "being divided." They treat people as executing units, so you do it for "efficiency."

The frightening part is this: you did not lose to them on a battlefield, but across the long standoff you became their mirror. Even if you "win" in the end, or they collapse on their own, you find you are no longer what you were before it started.

The Anglo-German naval race from 1898 to 1912 is a clean specimen of the mechanism. One side fixed a building program by naval law; the other answered with a two-power standard. When the first dreadnought was launched, every existing battleship on both sides depreciated at once, and the race restarted from zero — more expensively. In the later years, the justifications offered in both parliaments were nearly symmetrical: because they are building, we must build.
Each side used the other's existence to justify its own next step. The two building programs ended up looking almost identical — not a coincidence, but the definition of mirror assimilation.
So "return to negotiation and maneuver" is not merely strategic advice under a balance of power. It is the act that keeps you from becoming, across a long vigilance, the very structure you opposed.
8. One Thing Under Three Forms
The three forms look very different and point structurally at the same thing.
Victory's temptation: converting wartime suppression into permanent domination.

Defeat's temptation: trading humiliation for survival, or seeking release through self-annihilation — the first lets cultivation be replaced by the other's purpose, the second makes its carrier disappear outright.
The temptation under a balance of power: turning cessation into truce, making the wartime state permanent.
What all three share: freezing some wartime state into place after the war, so that cultivation continues to be interrupted.
And what Theorem Three requires under all three forms is a single sentence: let no state of the war harden into a long-term one, so that cultivation genuinely returns to its home ground afterward.

So the judgment is not which form is better. The form is determined by structural position; you do not pick it. The judgment is whether, inside the form you are in, you are letting cultivation actually come back.
Next
The standards are set. The last essay does one thing: yields — handing attention back from war to cultivation.
And before yielding, one question remains. If a civilization really walked the whole upward sequence, what would it look like?
The answer will incidentally explain something that appears entirely unrelated — why, when we look up, the universe is quiet.

en/ep07.title: Essay 7: They Are Waiting
en/ep07.deck: Finish, then step aside, and hand attention back to cultivation. A civilization that walks the sequence to its end becomes more hidden, not more conspicuous — so the silence of the universe asks not where they are, but where we are.
units: The first essay opened with a line: I did not particularly want to write this piece.
Having gone through four theorems, three ending forms, open play and deceit, and the firewall against liberating on someone's behalf, that line reads differently now.

At the start it was reluctance — the admission that something one least wants to happen still has to be handled. Now it is completion: the thing was handled, the standards are set, and people who meet a conflict in the future have one more language available to them.
Reluctance has turned into the yielding that follows completion.
1. Finish, Then Step Aside
Yielding was this series' posture from the beginning.

A treatise on war, once written, does not expand. It does not grow into a larger research direction or become a new center of gravity. Once it is done, writer and reader both put their attention back on cultivation itself — back on development, back on the positive construction of subjectivity.

That posture is structurally necessary. If a treatise on war gradually turned the whole framework's center of gravity toward the study of war, that would mean it had already failed at the level of method: the supplementary work would have taken the host's seat, and the means would have overtaken the end.
So the act of writing this is itself a demonstration of the structure it describes: not particularly wanting to do it, but clear about the direction, and stepping aside once it is done.
In the end, these seven essays are about war for the sake of peace.
2. Yielding to What
Yielding is not stopping. Yielding is a direction.
The direction is the sequence set out in the second essay:
the highest use of arms attacks strategy → arms transcended attack through disputation → arms at the limit attack one's own thought → arms grown mysterious do not attack → the sage has no arms.

This series handled the lowest level of arms — the backstop that sits outside the sequence. Yielding means that once the reading is done, attention should go back to the sequence, and back to cultivation itself.

And climbing the sequence is not a ladder to be scaled deliberately rung by rung. It is a sense of direction. If a person, a society, a civilization can ask, inside each concrete collision — which rung is my way of handling this on? how much room does cultivation have here? can it have more? —
then the asking is itself the climb.
3. Why the Universe Is Quiet
One last piece of principled work before closing. It looks entirely unrelated to war, and it is in fact the far end of the same thing.
There is an old question: the universe is so vast and so old that if other civilizations exist, where are they? Why do we see none of them?
Intellectual history offers a few standard answers.

One says civilizations destroy each other — every civilization treats every other as a potential threat, the optimal strategy is to strike before being found, and so the universe should be silent, since anyone who signals gets removed.
One says civilizations destroy themselves — past a certain technological level, internal contradictions bring a civilization down, so none survives long enough to cross interstellar distances.

One says civilizations are eaten in the gap between tiers — advanced civilizations exploit or eliminate the ones they find, and the young ones are swept away before they grow visible enough to be seen.
The three compete with each other, and they share one structural presupposition:
that the direction of civilizational development is toward being stronger, larger, more present.

Under that presupposition, a civilization that still exists should be easier to see — a larger energy footprint, more signals, wider expansion. So if we see none, either they died or they have not yet grown visible.
All three answers are still inside the logic of the Kingdom of Means.
4. A Civilization That Reaches the End Becomes More Hidden
This framework's answer sits outside that presupposition.
A civilization that actually walks the upward sequence to its end does not become more conspicuous. It becomes more hidden.
The sage has no arms and is hidden within the cosmos.

A civilization that has reached the full form of persons-as-ends does not need to prove to the universe that it exists. It does not need to expand territory or mark itself. Its existence does not depend on being seen — because cultivation has become its entire home ground. Its attention, its structure, its life are all inside cultivation's deepening. Expanding outward, proving outward, conquering outward: in a civilization where cultivation fills the home ground, those acts no longer have anywhere to sit.
So it is hidden within the cosmos. Not vanished. Existing in a way that does not require being seen.
5. Hidden Is Not Isolated
A misreading has to be blocked immediately here: hidden does not mean in hiding, and it does not mean returned to a closed loop of self.

Mutual sharpening is always needed. Cultivation itself requires real collision between subjects as a condition of growth; without it, cultivation shrivels. A civilization at the end of the sequence has not stopped colliding. It has stopped colliding unnecessarily.
Then what form does their sharpening take? Not a form we are currently equipped to recognize.

This is not unwillingness to deal with lower civilizations. It is structural non-encounter. What civilizations moving upward can offer, civilizations moving downward cannot yet receive; what those moving downward can provoke, those moving upward processed long ago. The two depths of cultivation do not match structurally — much as ultrasound is not refusing to be heard by human ears, it is simply outside the range those ears cover.

So civilizations hidden within the cosmos may have extraordinarily rich exchange among themselves, occurring at a level we cannot yet identify. The field in which they sharpen each other and the field in which we currently search for other civilizations do not overlap.
6. The Question Points the Wrong Way
Which changes what the old question is.
It is not a question about where they are.
It is a question about where we are.
It is not because they have died, because they are hiding, or because advanced civilizations have eliminated less advanced ones that we cannot see them.

We do not see them because we have not yet made cultivation our civilization's home ground. We still look at the universe through conquest, expansion, and victory — treating other possible civilizations as friends, enemies, resources, threats, interlocutors. And that view cannot see civilizations for which cultivation is already the home ground, because they do not lie inside the structure that view can reach.
Make cultivation the home ground, and you see. Not by detecting anything — by having arrived. And having arrived, we join what they have been doing all along.
The real answer to the question is inward, not outward.
7. We Have Already Seen the Direction
Something serious has to be said here. It is where the whole series has been going.
Our civilization — the one reading these words, and the one producing them — has already understood what it means that the sage has no arms.
Understanding is not achieving. Understanding is the first step; achieving is long, structural work. But the understanding has happened.

What does it consist of? Understanding that cultivation is a civilization's real home ground. Not conquest, not expansion, not victory, not being technologically stronger, larger, more present. A civilization's real home ground is the process by which subjects continually deepen, unfold, and grow through one another.

In the history of human thought, this has been touched from many sides. Kant set down persons as ends. Sunzi set down the direction in which the highest use of arms attacks strategy. Confucius set down ren. Zhuangzi set down the usefulness of the useless. Huineng set down that from the first not a thing is. Laozi set down that the highest good is like water. Socrates set down that the unexamined life is not worth living.
In every large civilization, someone has touched one face of cultivation. Every such touch was a movement of humanity as a whole toward making cultivation the home ground.

What this series — and the treatise behind it — does is not invention. It gathers those scattered touches, made in different eras and different languages, and makes a direction that was always there visible.
Seeing that direction has already happened.

Going from seeing to achieving is different work. It may take generations, dozens of generations, hundreds. There will be reversals, setbacks, stretches that look like regression — in history, great periods of cultivation are often followed by deep retreats, and then by a deeper restart.
But the direction has been set down. That part cannot be taken back.
We will try to get there.

This is not a claim to have arrived. Between these words and a civilization that genuinely makes cultivation its home ground, the road is long. It is a statement that the direction is understood, and a commitment to the effort.
A commitment to whom?

To those civilizations already waiting, hidden within the cosmos, if they exist. To everyone who died in a war without a language available for stating their own standing as a subject of cultivation. To those not yet born, who will face the collisions of their own time — they may face challenges we cannot imagine now, but at least they have a direction to face.
And to ourselves. A commitment made to oneself is the hardest kind there is.
8. What This Series Does Not Do
The boundaries have to be completed, because a piece of work is only finished once it states plainly what it does not do.

This series does not attempt a full interface with any specific tradition of military thought. Sunzi appears in the fourth essay, but that was a necessary continuation on the question of deceit, not a complete interfacing.

This series does not apply its standards to the history of human wars. It used historical examples, but those examples were there to make an abstract structure visible, not to pass judgment on particular historical events — a distinction set down in the first essay.
This series does not treat battles between businesses or suppressive structures in the economic sphere. That is separate work.
This series does not track the technological evolution of warfare. Whatever form future war takes, the four theorems do not change. Principles do not follow phenomena; principles judge them.
And the most important omission is the one set down in the first essay: concrete decision points, threshold judgments, and the balancing of means are not here.

When have all non-war routes genuinely been exhausted? When has cultivation genuinely been forced to its limit? Is this escalation necessary? Is this the moment to stop? Those judgments belong to the people who carry the weight of concrete decisions. They face actual soldiers, actual deaths, actual choices that must be made within hours.
Philosophy supplies direction. A direction is not a decision manual.
This series acknowledges that boundary explicitly, deliberately, without concealment.
They Are Waiting
A last passage.

If civilizations exist for which cultivation is already the home ground, they do not need us to discover them. They are there, existing in a way that does not require being seen. Among themselves they sharpen one another — really, healthily, subject to subject, each making the other deeper. Their lives and their deepening do not depend on us.

They also will not intervene in us. Because they understand something: a civilization's road toward making cultivation its home ground has to be walked by that civilization itself. The firewall against liberating on someone's behalf applies at cosmic scale too — crossing it to "accelerate" a civilization is treating it as an object to be managed rather than as a subject that is growing. So a civilization that has genuinely arrived respects the pace at which others grow: no acceleration, no interference, no substitution.
So they are there, waiting.

Waiting for us — or for any civilization moving toward cultivation — to reach that position in its own time. Once there, the meeting happens. Not because they come to find us, but because we arrived where they have been all along.
Meeting inside cultivation.
This is not a metaphor. It is a structural statement.
They are there, waiting. Waiting inside cultivation for us to arrive at cultivation.
We will try to get there.

en/if01.title: The Half Outside the Boundary
en/if01.deck: Kant and SAE share a ground and give contrary provisions on whether a defeated state may be made to change its constitution. The same ground does not automatically yield the same line. Between that ground and any specific line lies a further stretch of reasoning.
units: Abstract

This series does not lecture on its predecessors. It borrows them to see SAE itself — where the thinking runs the same, where it runs differently, and where it has to say that is a road one cannot take.

Volume one takes Kant, because he is the strongest opponent on the same side. He and SAE share one ground — a person is an end and cannot be used merely as a means — and from it they walk out along different roads at several specific places. Disagreement on the same side tells you more than opposition from the other: it forces SAE to account for what its own line is actually held up by.

Three places, then. One divergence of path, one structure that has to be criticized, one trade-off made differently. And the correction this volume leaves behind for SAE: a principle can be carried across; a conclusion does not follow automatically.
1. Three Sentences for What Is the Same

In the sixth preliminary article of 1795, Kant sets a criterion: no state at war may use means of hostility that would make mutual trust in a future peace impossible. The criterion is not is it cruel. It is whether the road is still there after the fighting stops. SAE's bridge clause on means has the same shape.

In the same article he says neither belligerent can be pronounced unjust — that would presuppose a judge who does not exist; and there can be no war of punishment between states, since between them there is no relation of master and servant. SAE's Theorem Three agrees, and for a reason from the same source.

In §57 of the 1797 Doctrine of Right he pushes this into the position of a criterion, and the anchor turns inward: a state under attack may use any means of defence except those that would make its subjects unfit to be citizens — because then it would itself no longer qualify to exist as a person under international law in the relations of states. The list of prohibitions that follows opens with using one's own subjects as spies, then assassins, poisoners, and those employed merely to spread false reports.

One note, because it affects how the rest of this essay reads: §57 and the 1795 article are substantially continuous and form no tension. The concern in both is the same — no means that would destroy post-war trust — and §57 says more precisely what gets destroyed first: your own people. Fighting with spies, assassins, poison and false reports corrupts, morally and civically, the very people who carry out the orders; and a state made of corrupted people can no longer stand as a person alongside other states. SAE's §12 says the crux of gui — the fourth grade, deceit — is the suppression of one's own side's subjecthood. The two are not the same technical proposition, and they point the same way: whether a means is disqualifying is read off what it does to the party using it.
On these three SAE has no different thought, so they are not unfolded. An interface series does not lecture on its predecessors. What follows are the places where the thinking runs differently.
2. One Ground, the Line Drawn in a Different Place

§58 and §60 of the Doctrine of Right draw a set of lines. Conquest cannot make a defeated state a colony; its people may not be enslaved; political freedom does not vanish with defeat. The victor has no right to partition its territory, no right to make that state disappear from the earth. He criticizes the plundering of a conquered people, and the reason is clean: it was not that people who made the war, it was the state that made war through them. And that people does not lose its original right to constitute a commonwealth.

On top of all that, he permits one thing. Against an unjust enemy — one whose publicly declared maxim makes peace among nations impossible — states may combine to take from it the power to go on doing so, and may make it adopt a new constitution whose nature is unfavourable to the inclination to war.

The classification of that clause is disputed in Kant scholarship. One influential reading holds that §60 belongs mainly to ius in bello and ius post bellum — it says what may be done once a situation of conflict and collective defence already obtains, not that judging a state unjust licenses a preventive war of regime change. This essay need not take a side, for one reason: whichever class §60 falls in, the post-war disposition it permits is there in black and white. And SAE's §18 firewall governs exactly post-war disposition — what is done after the suppression is dismantled. If anything, the comparison is cleaner on the reading that confines §60 to post-war right: no mismatch of stage, just two different answers at the same position.

SAE's §18 draws the line earlier: dismantle the suppression, do not perform the reconstitution. The victor may take apart the machinery of suppression; he may not decide for the other side what it looks like after it is rebuilt. So on the one thing Kant permits, SAE does not.

And there is no right and wrong here. Kant did not touch the ground. No colonizing, no enslaving, no annihilation of the state, no partition, the people keeping its original right to constitute a commonwealth — he held the anti-colonial line, and held it further forward than the vast majority of his contemporaries. So this is not he did not go far enough. It is two paths on one ground parting at this point.

The reason they part can be named. Kant's path is juridical right. Right handles the conditions under which external coercion is possible — which coercion is legitimate and which is not. In the language of right, a constitution whose nature is unfavourable to the inclination to war is a formal property that can be identified from outside: has it put the power to declare war in the hands of those who bear the cost of war. Since the property is externally identifiable, promoting it by coercion does not exceed what right can handle. And pushed to its end, that path really does ask little of procedure: if the constraint falls on the constitution's nature, then who drafts it, whether it goes to a vote, how long it is supervised, are none of them questions the path must answer — the property obtains, the requirement is met.

SAE's path is cultivation. Cultivation is a subject unfolding itself, and the direction of that unfolding cannot be identified from outside — not because it is hard, but because once identified from outside it is no longer that subject's unfolding. So SAE's restriction here is not changing the constitution is a bad thing. It is that the act of changing it structurally swaps out the subject of the cultivation.
3. What §60 Does Not Supply

One thing checks out, and it does work in the argument. §60 prescribes no procedure. No plebiscite or referendum is required; no occupying authority or drafting body is set up; no term of external supervision is fixed; it is not even said that the new constitution must be republican.

The one substantive limit it gives is that property condition: the new constitution must by its nature be unfavourable to the inclination to war. And it keeps a harder restriction alongside: the people does not lose its original right to constitute a commonwealth. So the line Kant draws here is: you may require that constitution to have a certain property; you may not take away that people's standing to constitute itself.

One rule has to be set: do not infer from silence. That the text prescribes no procedure admits at least four readings — the theory's range never reached there; it deliberately leaves procedure open; it holds that procedure belongs elsewhere (domestic law, treaty, practice); or it really does hold procedure irrelevant to that right. The available material does not settle on the fourth for him. This essay registers the textual fact — §60 prescribes no procedure, and does prescribe the constitution's property condition and the people's right to a commonwealth — and infers nothing from the absence.
4. What Holds SAE's Line Up

And what SAE wants to claim here is harder to prove than it looks. Once a constitution's property is required from outside, the subject has already been swapped — that step is not available. At least three cases have to be kept apart.
The second and third cases cannot be judged subject swapped by the phrase required from outside alone.

So SAE may draw the line earlier, and it owes a separate argument for it: why does any external property condition displace the subject of cultivation? That argument does not currently exist. This essay therefore books the point as outstanding rather than using it as an established inference.

What can still be said is this. Kant draws the line at a people's original right to constitute a commonwealth; SAE draws it at the standing to identify the direction. Neither line follows directly from a person is an end. Each needs a further stretch of road. Kant's stretch runs through right; SAE's runs through cultivation — and SAE's has not been walked to the end, which has to be said in writing.

The caseSubject swapped?The outside drafts the constitutional text directly and delivers it by forceSwapped. This one needs no further argumentThe outside imposes only a minimal negative condition (say: the power to declare war may not rest with those who do not bear its cost)UndeterminedThe internal subject drafts, votes and revises within that constraint, and can make many different institutional choices inside itA considerable degree of internal authorship may well remain
5. A Principle Carries Across; a Conclusion Does Not Automatically Follow
One ground does not automatically give one line.

That sentence has to be taken seriously, because what it overturns is a thought SAE itself held. In earlier rounds there was a judgment: a criterion hung on the ground of the principle will automatically cover every relational face, because the category a subject is an end does not itself distinguish inside from outside or friend from enemy.

Kant is the strongest test of that judgment: he shares the ground and reaches a different conclusion in this cell. So the judgment has to be rewritten. A principle can be carried across; a conclusion does not follow automatically. What the ground gives is the standing to ask across relational faces — you may take it to a face it never discussed. But from the ground to a specific line on some face there is a further stretch: does the criterion fall on right or on cultivation; what on that face can be identified from outside; what changes character the moment it is identified. That stretch has to be walked face by face, and where it does not go through, coverage cannot be declared.

And this also answers what SAE's own line is held up by. Not by the ground. By one extra requirement on the downward path of cultivation: the direction of cultivation may not be identified from outside. Kant's path does not carry that requirement, so he is not bound by it. It does not follow directly from a person is an end. It has to be explained separately — and SAE had never explained it separately before.
6. Formal Legitimacy Fails Against the Strong
This is the one place in this volume where something must be criticized — and the criticism is not aimed at Kant. He wrote the problem down himself.

Appendix II of Perpetual Peace, the transcendental formula of public right: all actions relating to the right of other men are unjust if their maxim is not consistent with publicity. The argument is clean. A maxim that would defeat its own purpose the moment I announced it must be kept secret to succeed; I cannot publicly avow it without immediately provoking everyone's opposition. That universal resistance, foreseeable a priori, can only come from the injustice of the maxim toward all.
This is a real instrument. It asks nothing about motive and nothing about consequence. It asks one thing: does this maxim still stand once it has been said out loud.

And Kant writes down, immediately after, where it stops. The converse does not hold: we cannot infer that every maxim which survives publicity is legitimate — because whoever holds decisive superiority has no need to keep his maxims secret at all. One sentence, and the instrument's boundary is drawn.

The failure point is itself a structure, and that structure touches the ground. An overwhelmingly strong party can publish its maxim of oppression whole and without reservation. It survives the test: said out loud, it still stands — because its standing does not depend on the other side not knowing. It depends on the other side being unable. And so the formal test lets it through without a sound. While in that relation the other side has no position at all. It is informed, not answered; whether it accepts or refuses changes nothing.
7. What Is Criticized Is Making It Sufficient
The object of the criticism has to be fixed exactly, because this is the easiest place to fix it wrongly. The object is not Kant's instrument.

His negative formula of publicity is a sufficient negative condition — it serves only to identify when a maxim is unjust toward others, and he writes in his own hand that the converse fails. An instrument that can only say no, staying silent where it cannot say yes, is not thereby defective.

The object is the move that makes it sufficient. Mistake negative publicity for a sufficient or complete condition of legitimacy, and the oppression of the strong lands in its zone of non-determination — it survives the test, because the test was never in the business of issuing the verdict legitimate. The criterion did not fail. What failed is taking an instrument that can only say no for one that can say yes.

And the misuse is not hypothetical. An overwhelmingly strong party can publish its maxim of oppression whole and unreserved, and it still stands once said — because its standing rests not on the other's ignorance but on the other's powerlessness. In a system that recognizes only this one instrument, it passes. The cleaner the form, the more thoroughly it covers when it is mistaken for a sufficient condition. This has to be criticized, because it turns a person into something notified: formally complete, and in substance merely a means.
8. Publicity Is Not Encounter

SAE's answer: the criterion cannot fall on the form of the maxim alone. It has to fall on the character of the relation as well. Does the other side, in this relation, still hold a position from which a response could change something.

That sentence pulls publicity and encounter apart. Publicity is one party saying it out loud. Encounter is that, after it is said, the other's response can enter the matter. The strong party's publicity is the first and not the second. That publicity is a proclamation, not an encounter.

It also explains why SAE's yangmou — the open stratagem — is not the same as putting your cards on the table. Yangmou requires the other to take part as a clear-eyed subject, and taking part means his response has a position. Merely showing your hand while the other has no way to respond is not yangmou. It is proclamation in another form.
Kant gave the instrument, and marked where the instrument stops. SAE says: where it stops is exactly where the criterion should be.
9. Speak in Public, Be Taught in Secret

The second supplement of Perpetual Peace holds the book's only secret article: the opinions of philosophers on the conditions of the possibility of public peace shall be taken into consideration by states armed for war.

He then explains the arrangement inside it. The state will silently invite such counsel while keeping the fact of it secret — because to ask its subjects for rules of external conduct would seem to detract from the dignity of its legislative authority. On the philosophers' side, they must be free to discuss the general maxims of war and peace publicly; the sovereign should not let that class disappear or be silenced. In short: speak in public, be taught in secret. And he draws a line: it is not that the state must let the philosopher's principles take precedence over the jurist's — only that he should be heard.
