SAE's Theorem Four requires that a warring party cannot but be questioned, and the questioning has to reach four layers: does questioning exist; does it reach the core of decision; is the questioner protected; does the questioning actually affect the decision.

Read Kant's article against those four. Questioning: yes. Reaching the core of decision: only adjacent — taken into consideration gives a duty to consider, not a position inside the procedure of decision. The questioner is locally protected: public speech may not be forbidden and the class may not be silenced, but there is no protection from reprisal and no procedural guarantee. Actual effect on the decision is not secured: no precedence does not mean no effect, and being heard does not guarantee a change. So it is a local mechanism, and it is not closed.
10. A Different Trade-off, Not a Right and a Wrong

The point is that Kant's misgiving is real, and he put it on paper: the state holds that admitting it needs instruction detracts from its dignity. He is facing a genuine trade-off — the mechanism, or the mechanism being acknowledged. He chose the first, and the price is that it cannot be seen. In his context, insisting on public acknowledgment might have meant no opening at all.

SAE chose the second, and its reason is structural too: an unacknowledged questioning cannot hold up layers three and four. Whether the questioner is protected, and whether the questioning really affects the decision, both depend on the thing itself being visible — an invisible questioning cannot be verified, and so cannot be found out when it is hollowed.

Two trade-offs, each with its price. Kant's price is that efficacy is unsecured. SAE's price is that in some contexts this requirement may keep the mechanism from being built at all. Nothing here is criticized, because the ground was not touched: Kant did not abolish questioning. He put it somewhere it could survive.

One thing is worth writing down all the same. Even the man who laid this ground, when he came to write the mechanism of questioning onto a state armed for war, hid it in a secret article. Not because he was insufficiently thorough. Because this requirement, the moment it lands on an actual structure of power, meets a specific resistance — dignity. Kant is the one who wrote that resistance out, which is why its shape is visible from him. Whether the resistance is universal across all traditions, the sample of this series is not yet complete, and no claim is made.
11. The Half Outside the Boundary

Three places: one divergence of path, one structure that had to be criticized, one trade-off made differently. They show the same thing. SAE and Kant share a ground, and the ground does not decide everything. Walking down from a person is an end, the choice of right or of cultivation parts into different lines at specific places, different landing points for the criterion, different trade-offs.

What this volume leaves SAE is not knowledge about Kant. It is a correction of SAE's own: a principle can be carried across; a conclusion does not follow automatically. The §18 firewall does not come straight down from the ground. It depends on one extra requirement along the path of cultivation — that the direction of cultivation may not be identified from outside — and that requirement had never been stated on its own.

The half outside the boundary in the title means this. Not that Kant wrote no criterion for conduct in war — he did. Not that right cannot handle subjects — legal personality, civic standing, future trust, he handled all of them. It is the layer that remains unsettled by those even after all of them are protected: whether a subject, inside the relation, still holds the position to question, refuse, revise, respond, and go on unfolding itself.
That layer lies outside the boundary of right. It is where cultivation takes over.
Materials, and Three Things Booked

Kant's Perpetual Peace is cited from the Mary Campbell Smith translation of 1903 — preliminary articles three, five and six; the first definitive article; the second supplement; appendix II. The Doctrine of Right is cited from the Akademie German — §57 (VI:347–348), §58 (VI:348–349), §59 (VI:349), §60 (VI:349–350). Chinese renderings are the author's own. Two version warnings stand: §60 opens with a parenthetical limiting the right against an unjust enemy in the kind of means while leaving quantity and degree unbounded, and a nineteenth-century English translation may have inverted quality and quantity there — wherever §60 is involved the Akademie German governs; and the Doctrine of Right has known scholarly disputes over editing and paragraph attribution, though §57–§60 were not found to fall inside them.

Two things are downgraded here rather than claimed. That §60 prescribes no procedure is registered as a textual fact only, with nothing inferred from it. And the step any external property condition displaces the subject of cultivation has not been established by argument in this volume, so it is booked as outstanding: SAE may draw its line earlier than Kant, and it needs an independent argument to do so, and that argument does not yet exist. Until it is finished, the claim here is only that each line needs a further stretch of road — not that SAE's stretch has been walked.

One interpretive dispute is left unchosen — whether §60 is an independent exception in ius ad bellum or belongs mainly to ius in bello and ius post bellum — since neither reading affects the argument. And one debt is booked without an answer. Kant's exception for a divided state covers the case where a country splits in two, each part claiming to be an independent state representing the whole. When both parts claim in the first person to represent the whole, which bearing-position does §18's do not perform the other side's reconstitution for it protect? How is an outside actor to tell, without the telling itself completing the legislation for the whole? Kant gives when assistance stops counting as interference. What he does not give, and SAE has not given either, is how to identify the legitimate bearer among competing claims of representation.

This series keeps its own correction records in the body rather than repairing them silently, for a reason: a framework that requires cannot but be questioned must be the first thing questioned; and a text that shows no sign of ever having erred gives its reader no way to judge how its determinations were reached.

en/if02.title: Who Gave the Authorisation
en/if02.deck: Clausewitz and On Protracted War share one form of constraint: war is authorised by an external political purpose and constrained by it. And that form cannot restrain the authoriser itself. The purpose may expand on its own in the course of the war.
units: Abstract
This volume runs on two layers, and the point of it is that they cannot be run together.

Layer one: authorisation. Clausewitz and On Protracted War give constraints on war that share one form — war is authorised by an external political purpose and is therefore bound by it. SAE agrees with the content of both. But the form carries a premise neither states on its own: that the authoriser is itself stable, bounded, and does not expand. Neither authoriser satisfies it. So the form has a common limit — it cannot hold back the authoriser itself.

That limit is registered as a limit of the form, not as an internal failure. Neither party ever claimed its theory could bind the political purpose itself, so your constraint cannot hold back the authoriser is no internal criticism of either.

Layer two: the carrier. Machiavelli does not supply a third specimen of the same kind. He supplies a second-order stress test on layer one: even where the authoriser is itself constrained, the carrier that executes may form a war-interest of its own. Layer one asks whether the authoriser will move. Layer two asks whether, even with the authoriser still, the men who execute it will move on their own. Each layer has its own solutions and problems it cannot solve — and one layer's solution does not solve the other's problem.
1. War Is Sent Out, So It Must Report Back

Clausewitz and On Protracted War both hold that war should not swell on its own, and the constraint each gives takes the same form: war was sent out, so it has to go back and account to the thing that sent it.

Book Eight, chapter six B of On War puts the form most completely. War is nothing but a continuation of political intercourse with the admixture of other means; the phrase with other means is there to show at once that this political intercourse is not stopped by the war itself, does not change into something wholly different, but continues in its essence. And then: war has its own grammar, but not its own logic. Followed by the sentence that completes the form — war can never be separated from political intercourse; separate them in any way and the threads of the relations are to some extent broken, and what stands before us is a thing without object, meaningless.
Grammar of its own, logic from outside. That is the form.

On Protracted War is the one worth the closest look on this layer, because it writes the stopping condition down in plain words. War is the continuation of politics, put symmetrically: politics is bloodless war, war is bloody politics. And the stopping rule is indexed to the political purpose — the political obstacle removed and the political purpose attained, the war stops; the obstacle not fully removed and the purpose not fully attained, the war goes on. The stopping condition is not military opportunity exhausted and not the enemy destroyed. It is whether that political purpose has been completed.

So the two share one form: war is authorised by an external political purpose and is therefore bound by it. SAE agrees with both constraints. War really should not swell on its own. This is a real overlap, not a courtesy.
2. Machiavelli Is Not a Third Specimen

Machiavelli does not stand alongside the first two, and the reason has to be set out first. Clausewitz and On Protracted War give the authorisation and constraint of war by an external political purpose. Book One of The Art of War gives the incentive structure of the executing carrier. The two are not of one type — the first asks what authorises war, the second asks what the men who carry out war live on. Fold the second into the first, and two different levels get pressed into one.
His correct position here is the second-order stress test: even where the authoriser is itself constrained, the carrier that executes may form a war-interest of its own.

The material for registering it: in Book One, Machiavelli has Fabrizio Colonna argue that a well-ordered republic never allowed any of its citizens or subjects to practise war as a trade. The reason is not efficiency. It is a chain of incentives whose starting point is that the trade has no ordinary livelihood in peacetime, so those who depend on it must wish peace not to exist.

Two limits go with it. The speaker is Fabrizio, not Machiavelli in his own voice — the book is a dialogue. And what is forbidden is private livelihood, not knowledge of war: chapter fourteen of The Prince, in the author's own voice, says a prince should make the art of war his principal study. The two do not conflict.
3. Why the Two Layers Cannot Be Run Together

Layer one asks: will the authoriser move? Answer: yes. Layer two asks: even if the authoriser does not move, will the men who execute it move on their own? Answer: yes — as soon as their livelihood is tied to war.

The two have different solutions, and that is exactly what this volume needs from them. Layer one's problem has no solution here — the legitimacy of the authoriser is supplied from elsewhere. Layer two's problem does have one, and Machiavelli gives it: let no one practise war as a trade.

So this volume does not count him as a failed case. What he gives on layer two is a workable disposition. And the converse holds too: adopt his restriction, and layer one's problem is still there — the survival of a republic can equally demand conquest abroad.

Each layer has its own solutions and problems it cannot solve; and one layer's solution does not solve the other's problem. That sentence is all this volume takes from Machiavelli. The full treatment of layer two belongs to the question of how a means reworks the party using it, and that is not this volume's business.
4. The Other End of the Rope Is Moving

The form war is constrained by an external purpose carries a premise: that the authoriser is itself stable, bounded, and does not expand. If the authoriser can enlarge its goals in the course of things, then war must not exceed the purpose constrains only the distance between war and purpose — not how far the purpose itself has moved. The shape of the constraint is a rope, and the other end of the rope is moving.
Neither party states the premise on its own, because in each of their contexts it was too natural to state. And neither authoriser satisfies it.

Reason of state can be expansionist. Clausewitz's political purpose is the state's political purpose, and a state's political purpose can perfectly well be acquire more. War must not depart from the political purpose still holds — it merely constrains war not to exceed what the expansion requires. It cannot hold back the expansion.

A political purpose can upgrade itself. A political line redefines its goals in execution; that is not a betrayal of the line, it is the line's normal evolution. And after the redefinition, war is the continuation of politics still holds. What continues is the new politics.
5. The Clearer the Stopping Line, the Plainer What It Hangs On

And On Protracted War, precisely because it writes the stopping condition in plain words, shows the problem most clearly. Its rule is: political purpose attained, war stops. That is the only stopping condition among these two accounts on this layer that can be quoted, questioned, and checked afterwards — in that sense it is the best of the two.

And that plain stopping condition moves as the political purpose moves. Redefine the purpose and the stopping line shifts with it, while the rule political purpose attained, war stops needs not one word changed. So this is not a counter-example. It is the strongest positive example: the more clearly the stopping condition is written, the more plainly one sees what it hangs on. A plain sentence hung on something movable is still movable.

So the form has a common limit: it cannot hold back the authoriser itself. And the registration matters. This is uncovered / a limit of the form, not an internal failure. To call it a failure point would require first showing that the party had claimed some goal or criterion of its own — and neither ever claimed its theory could bind the political purpose itself. Clausewitz's theory sets out to explain what war is and how it stands to policy; On Protracted War answers how one particular war is to be fought. Your constraint cannot hold back the authoriser is an internal criticism of neither, because neither took that job. The object of the proposition is the form, not the men.

And this is not two men's separate oversight. Two different authorisers give the same limit, which says the limit does not lie in the choice of authoriser but in the form of taking authorisation. It takes both side by side to see it: read Clausewitz alone and you will think his reason of state was insufficiently pure; read On Protracted War alone and you will think it a problem with one particular line. Two systems with unrelated sources landing at the same place say the place is structurally determined.
6. One Objection, and How It Is Rightly Handled

The objection: Clausewitz was not naive. He knew policy could be bad policy; he says in the same chapter that if the policy itself is wrong, no correctness of military means makes up for it. So he foresaw that the authoriser is unconstrained, and simply held that this belongs to political science and not to the study of war.

The objection holds, and this volume accepts it. To say putting it outside the scope is exactly how the failure happens is a quibble: assigning a problem elsewhere is a legitimate declaration of range. This series makes heavy use of range declarations itself — silence on everything at the execution layer — so applying the same standard to a predecessor is the minimum.

So what this volume says narrows to one independently checkable sentence: after that declaration of range, what can the remaining constraint do, and what can it not. It can keep war from exceeding a given political purpose. It cannot make that political purpose itself constrained. Neither sentence is a criticism of Clausewitz. The first is his achievement; the second is what he expressly put outside. What is pointed out is only this: for someone who wants war constrained, this form alone is not enough — and that has nothing to do with whether his theory succeeds.
The correction makes the proposition steadier rather than weaker: it now needs no author's oversight, and denies no author's declaration of range.
7. The End of the Path

Ludendorff walks this path to its end: he swaps the authoriser from politics to the national will, and the criterion of the national will is itself. He expressly inverts Clausewitz's primacy of politics — politics obeys the commander, and the whole life of the nation obeys the war.

The consequences follow straight from the limit above. An authoriser that is its own criterion cannot say when to stop — the object of the war becomes the survival of the nation itself, which can terminate only in one side being destroyed in the sense of survival. It cannot tolerate any mechanism that tests it. And it cannot be falsified by any outcome.

The nature of the evidence has to be written down. The inference is drawn from the structure of the form, not from any particular formulation in Total War; the first-hand text was not obtained for this series, and the passages that would have turned on its specific wording did not pass verification and are not used. That material has been moved out of the release package as an isolated research item.
8. Cultivation Cannot Authorise Its Own Abolition
SAE's Theorem Two also constrains the widening of war: every widening has to pass the criterion again, and cannot carry on automatically because the last one passed.
Theorem Two does not take its authorisation from an external purpose. Its criterion comes from cultivation, and cultivation cannot authorise its own abolition.

A political purpose can demand that everything be sacrificed for it, including the very people it was meant to protect. A republic's survival can demand that citizens be turned into a supply of soldiers. A line can demand that individuals submit all the way down. Each of these demands is self-consistent in its own logic: an authoriser is entitled to dispose of what it authorises. Cultivation has no such entitlement, and the reason is categorial. Cultivation is not a goal. It is the very thing of a subject unfolding itself. A criterion that demands the abolition of that unfolding abolishes its own condition of holding. It is not that it violates cultivation. It is structurally impossible to say.

From which one operating discipline follows, for SAE itself: the criterion may not be hung on any particular good thing. The state's security, the republic's freedom, the people's liberation — hang it on one of those and you have an authoriser; and once you have an authoriser you have something it cannot hold back.

The discipline applies to SAE, and applies uncomfortably. It means SAE cannot say our criterion is there to protect the oppressed — that would make the interest of the oppressed the authoriser, and it can expand like any other. A criterion can only be a criterion.
9. A Criterion and a Reason to Mobilise Are Not One Thing

One thing is easily written down as a cost of that discipline, and it is not a cost. The discipline seems to make SAE's criterion hard to mobilise with: for the homeland, for liberation can be shouted, can send people to die; cultivation cannot authorise its own abolition cannot.
The difficulty's premise does not hold. The false premise is that a criterion and a reason to mobilise must be the same thing. Separate four layers and the difficulty dissolves.

A particular good can mobilise. What it cannot do is acquire, on its own, the standing to begin a war, to widen one, or to be exempt from review. What the discipline blocks was never people fight for their homes. It is the phrase "for their homes" being taken to replace the threshold. A reason to mobilise enters the first layer and does not enter the second; it does not impersonate authorisation.

So the genuinely open question is not "the criterion cannot mobilise," but this: how to let particular reasons for mobilising enter public action without impersonating the standing to authorise — a checkable division of labour between the language of mobilisation and the procedure of authorisation. That is a doable problem, not a dead end.

LayerWhat goes in itReason to mobiliseHome, freedom, particular people, a particular situationCondition of authorisationTheorem One's structural thresholdLimits on meansTheorem Two, Theorem Three, the bridge clause on meansReviewTheorem Four
10. Where the People Stand in the Trinity

End of Book One, chapter one of On War: war is a wonderful trinity, composed of primordial violence, hatred and enmity — to be regarded as a blind natural force; of chance and probability; and of its subordinate instrumental character. The first belongs mainly to the people, the second to the commander and his army, the third to the government.

The arrangement leaves the people, in principle, without standing to question. The trouble is not that he put them in. It is where he put them. The people are the source of the war's energy, not its judge — and the consequence is structural: a corner constituted by blind impulse cannot be asked anything. You cannot demand reasons of a natural force. SAE's Theorem Four requires that a warring party cannot but be questioned, and that the questioning come from inside. Clausewitz's model has no such position.

This is not a belittling, and that has to be granted. Part of why he puts the people in that corner is that he had seen the mobilisation of the French Revolution — what he saw was a real, enormous force that had not existed before. His model describes that force accurately. What it does not describe is whether that force can ask a question.
11. Step Out of the Man, Into the Role

Book Three, on the military virtue of an army: to step out of this man and into the role that war assigns us to play — this is the form military virtue takes in the individual. And he adds that this virtue is a definite moral force, like any instrument whose effect can be calculated.
This sets the executor's no longer existing as a person, but as a role, up as a positive quality — and that touches a person is an end on one's own side.

It has to be put precisely. He is not praising coldness; he is describing how a good army actually works, and the description has an empirical basis — a unit that holds formation under fire really is acting by role rather than by individual reaction. The point of contact is the step of setting it up as a quality. Describing a phenomenon and setting it up as something to be pursued are two things, and he does the second: military virtue is a moral force an army ought to have, one that can be cultivated and can be calculated. The own-side half of the second formula is abolished there.
12. Friction: Two Faces of One Coin
Friction is usually taken to be Clausewitz's gift to SAE. It is — and it is at the same time something else, which has to be said first.

In war everything is very simple, but the simplest thing is difficult. These difficulties accumulate and produce a friction no one who has not seen war can accurately imagine. He gives the example of a traveller changing horses: at dusk you reckon on the last two stages, four or five leagues, nothing much; and at the second-to-last post there are no horses, or bad ones; then hills, bad roads, darkness — and after great trouble you reach the next stage to find wretched accommodation. Friction is the one concept that broadly corresponds to what distinguishes real war from war on paper.

But he says where friction comes from, very specifically, and that sentence changes everything. The military machine — the army and all belonging to it — is in fact simple, and appears on that account easy to manage. But we should bear in mind that no part of it is in one piece, that it is composed entirely of individuals, each of which keeps up its own friction in all directions. And then: a battalion is always composed of a number of men, the least important of whom, if chance so ordains, may occasion delay or even disorder.

Friction comes from this: an army is composed of individuals, and each individual has a direction of his own. And immediately after the description of friction, he writes the remedy. A powerful iron will overcomes this friction; it crushes the obstacles, but it also crushes the machine along with them.
The remedy he gives for friction and the definition he gives of military virtue point at one variable: how much of his own direction is left in the executor.

A stronger claim is not available, and has to be ruled out first. Someone will say: if friction comes from individuals each having their own direction, then reducing friction is reducing those directions — so an executor who has successfully stepped out of himself into the role no longer produces friction. That last sentence cannot be had, for two reasons.

First, friction is not one thing. The sources he lists fall into at least three classes — physical conditions; conditions of information and stamina; and individuals each having their own direction. Only the third bears on the executor's position as a subject. An executor wholly inside the role still meets bad roads, wrong intelligence and fatigue. He does not stop producing friction. He stops producing the third class. Second, no longer produces is a universal claim, and there is no material for it. Whether a man in the role never again hesitates, never adjusts by his own understanding, never pauses when orders and what he sees conflict — that is an empirical question about people. This volume makes no judgement on it, and Clausewitz supplies no evidence.

So the only thing claimed is what can be read off the text: on the third class of friction, his remedy and his definition of virtue point the same way — reduce how much of himself is left in the executor. That is coherent in his own text, not stitched together here: friction is diagnosed in Book One, virtue prescribed in Book Three, and on the third class their directions coincide.
13. Three Classes of Friction

SAE accepts the concept, and it fills a gap of SAE's own. The four theorems are all at the layer of principle, and they assume by default that a criterion once set can be applied. §3 concedes the lightness of philosophy and the weight of the executor, but that is a concession of posture — it grants that the executor's task is harder without saying where the difficulty lies. Friction supplies that: at the front the criterion is not violated, it is worn away. Delayed information, distorted orders, fatigue, fear, weather, terrain — each degrades the input conditions for judging is widening now unavoidable. The criterion is still there. What is needed to judge it is not.

But SAE refuses his remedy, and not on moral grounds. Part of friction is not a defect to be eliminated, and that part is exactly the mark of the executor still existing as a subject. The narrowing has to be stated, because friction is very easily equated wholesale with subjecthood — and it is not one thing.

Only by folding the three into one does one arrive at friction at zero means the parts have been reduced to parts. That inference holds for the third class alone. So: the third class cannot be eliminated without abolishing the executor's position as a subject. The first two can be reduced, and reducing them abolishes no one.

And his own remedy still has to be criticized, because what he gives is a remedy that does not classify: a powerful iron will overcomes this friction — it does not distinguish whether what is to be crushed is bad weather or a subordinate raising an objection. And the half-sentence he himself wrote states the price of not classifying: it crushes the obstacles, but it also crushes the machine along with them. So what is criticized is not that he wanted friction reduced. It is that the remedy does not classify. He saw the price and took it for a price that must be paid. SAE says: for the third class, that is not a price. That is the abolition of the thing to be protected.

SourceCharacterWeather, terrain, equipment failure, road conditionsNothing to do with subjecthood. Eliminating them abolishes no one's judgementDelayed information, distorted transmission of orders, fatigueIntermediate. Partly reducible by technique and training; reducing it abolishes no judgementIndividuals each having their own direction — hesitating, questioning, refusing, adjusting by their own understandingThis is subjecthood itself
14. The Criterion Must Be Internalized Before the Friction

The third class cannot be eliminated without abolishing the executor's position as a subject, and all three classes wear away the conditions for applying the criterion. So that road cannot be walked by eliminating friction. What remains is: the criterion has to be internalized before the friction, not computed on the battlefield.
Deepening cultivation in peacetime is not only the accumulation of national strength. It is making the criterion into something that can be drawn on without on-site calculation.

What the inference does not claim has to be written down: it does not claim internalization guarantees correct judgement, and it does not claim people who have internalized the criterion will err in the same direction. What it claims is that some class of question can still be perceived, raised, and enter adjudication under pressure — and that is the only form in which a criterion still works outside its range.

A community that only starts wondering is this right once it is on the battlefield will have its criterion worn off, because that is precisely the moment when information is worst, time shortest, fear greatest. A community that has grown the criterion in during peacetime cannot have it worn off, because there is nothing there that needs computing. And this is taken from Clausewitz: he described the resistance; SAE turned it into a requirement on peacetime.
15. Left Unresolved in This Volume

SAE's criterion is hard to mobilise with is not an unresolved item — the difficulty's premise does not hold. What is genuinely open is a different question: how to let particular reasons for mobilising enter public action without impersonating the standing to authorise. This volume does not answer it, and it is a doable problem.

And one lesson on method goes with it: this series had previously taken this one cannot be filtered out as evidence that a boundary was working, when the actual reason it could not be filtered out was that the question itself had been put wrongly. A question that cannot be filtered out may be evidence that the boundary works — or evidence that the question was badly written.

Internalization handles only cases the criterion already covers. Meet a new situation it does not cover and friction's wear applies in full, with the judge in the worst conditions. That family of problems has been settled by division rather than centrally: the moment the criterion is most needed is the moment judging conditions are worst is placed wholly outside the scope — it belongs to executive judgement, outside this series' range, and is acknowledged rather than booked as unresolved. The criterion must be internalizable stays inside — it is a question about how criteria are written, and internalization there has an exact meaning: move the criterion from the condition-subtracting end to the condition-adding end in advance, because on a battlefield there is no time to subtract.

And the trinity leaves the people without standing to question — while SAE has given no replacement model. In wartime, where does questioning come from, who protects it, how is it kept from being treated as sapping morale? This volume does not answer, and the question bears directly on the practical operability of Theorem Four.

en/if03.title: The Hand Is Being Reworked by What It Holds
en/if03.deck: Kant, Arendt, Machiavelli and SAE each supply one mechanism by which a means reworks the party that wields it — and the four do not contain one another. Setting them side by side reveals a specific blind spot.
units: Abstract

Kant, Arendt, Machiavelli and SAE each give a mechanism for one and the same thing: a means reworks the party using it. The four act at different places and at different times, and none of them contains the others — each has cases the other three do not cover.

What this volume does not claim: that their coverages are disjoint, or that SAE's is the narrowest. What is proved is mutual non-containment, not disjointness; and the four have heterogeneous domains, so there is no common ruler on which to rank them by width.

What is to be kept is one specific blind spot: §12 binds disqualification to information asymmetry, so an arrangement conducted in the open, with the executor fully informed, whose position as a subject is nonetheless abolished, gets no verdict from that criterion.

Three can be taken up, each differently. And the four together compose four angles of check for a list SAE cannot make on its own — but the four questions have to be preceded by a gate on the ground, because they screen what a means does to its user and cannot screen what an arrangement does to a particular person.
1. Four Mechanisms, Side by Side

Only by putting the four side by side do their differences become visible. That comparison is the main move of this volume. Separately each looks like common sense; together it shows that they do not govern the same thing.

Kant: vices get carried into the state of peace. The sixth preliminary article forbids assassins, poisoners, breach of capitulation, incitement to treason. He gives six reasons, and the least-quoted is the sixth: these infernal arts are already base in themselves and, once employed, do not long remain within the limits of war. Take the use of spies — here one merely takes advantage of another's dishonesty; but such vices, once encouraged, cannot in the nature of things be rooted out, and will be carried over into the state of peace, where their presence will utterly destroy the purpose of that state. Note why he names spies. He writes it himself: here one merely takes advantage of another's dishonesty — he knows this is the most harmless-looking of the family, and picks it for exactly that reason. If even this one spills over, the heavier ones need no arguing.

Arendt: violence destroys power, it never creates power. She defines power as the capacity to act in concert — power belongs to a group and exists only while the group holds together. Violence is instrumental: it needs an external purpose to justify it, and its efficacy grows with the improvement of the instrument, independently of the number who hold it. Hence her judgement: violence can destroy power, but it can never create it; a regime that rules by violence has thereby shown that it has lost power. The time is immediate — not use it long enough and it spoils, but consumed in the very moment of use, because resorting to violence is itself the sign that the capacity to act in concert no longer suffices.

Machiavelli: those who live by war must wish war to happen. In Book One of The Art of War, Fabrizio Colonna argues that a well-ordered republic never allowed any citizen or subject to practise war as a trade — and what he gives is a chain, not a sentence. The trade has no ordinary livelihood in peacetime, so those who depend on it must wish peace not to exist. That incentive produces plunder: robbery, fraud, violence and killing are structurally attached to the trade. A commander's standing and income depend on war, so he has an incentive to deceive his employer to prolong it. When peace comes and such men are dismissed, they readily turn to armed adventuring and live by pillage. Whence a constitutional trilemma: a prince keeping professional soldiers in peacetime must go on fighting, maintain them indefinitely, or face a body of armed men whose livelihood has vanished. And loyalty attaches to the commander, not to the commonwealth.

SAE: the crux of gui is the suppression of one's own side's subjecthood. §12 says deceit is disqualifying not because it deceives the enemy but because maintaining an information asymmetry requires using one's own executors as instruments. If the executor knew the whole picture, the asymmetry could not be held; so to use deceit you must first keep your own people in the dark. One registration goes with it: the four-grade scale used here — mou, covert stratagem, open stratagem, deceit — had part of its legitimacy resting on a finding since withdrawn, that Sunzi had already made a similar distinction. The withdrawal is in volume six. Re-arguing the scale is not the interface series' business; it belongs to §12 itself, and this volume uses it before that argument is complete.

Where it actsTimeWhat it depends onKantthe climate of one's own communityafter the warthe irreversibility of habitArendtpower itselfimmediatepower = the capacity to act in concertMachiavellian interest group inside the social structurelong-termlivelihood tied to warSAE §12the executor's position as a subject on one's own sideduring the waran information asymmetry requires the executor not to know
2. Non-Containment Is Not a Ranking by Width

The four do not contain one another: each has cases the other three do not cover, so none can replace the rest. This has to be put precisely — what is proved is non-containment, not disjointness. A technique may perfectly well depend on information asymmetry, build a professional carrier, spill over into peacetime, and displace concerted action all at once. The four are not a partition. They are four angles of check with overlapping regions and regions of their own.

And the ranking SAE's is the narrowest does not hold either: the four have heterogeneous domains — climate, power, interest group, executor's position — and there is no common ruler on which to rank them by width.

Each one's blind spot can be named. Kant's cannot check the immediate case. A means genuinely used once, genuinely forming no habit, gets no verdict — and only once is a judgement one can sincerely believe in war. Arendt's cannot check means that do not use violence. Deception, bribery, blockade, information manipulation fall outside her definition — and those are among the most commonly used means today. Machiavelli's cannot check the case with no professional body. An army raised for the occasion and disbanded after produces no one who lives by war. SAE's cannot check means that need no information asymmetry. A cruelty conducted in the open, with the executor fully informed, gets no verdict from §12.

So the thing to keep is weaker and more exact: §12's criterion is bound to the single variable of information asymmetry, so there exists a class of arrangement it cannot reach — no asymmetry, and the position as a subject abolished all the same. That sentence needs no judgement about relative width at all.
3. That Child
There is a ready example, and this volume sets it out in full because the later sections use it repeatedly.

From Nitobe Inazō's Bushido (1899), the chapter on loyalty, the story of Sugawara no Michizane. Michizane is exiled; his enemies mean to root out his line, and find his young son hidden in the village school kept by a former retainer, Genzō. The order comes down: on a certain day, deliver this boy's head. What Genzō thinks of is a substitute — and just then a new pupil arrives, of the same age as his lord's son and of similar appearance, brought by a mother of noble bearing.

Nitobe inserts one line here: the mother and the boy himself were equally aware of the resemblance; in the privacy of their home, both had already laid themselves on the altar. On the day, the official who comes to verify the head is that boy's own father; he calmly checks the features one by one and pronounces the head genuine. That evening, crossing his own threshold, he says to his wife: Rejoice, our darling son has been of use to his lord.

There is no information asymmetry anywhere in it. The parents know, the child knows, the teacher knows, and the official verifying the head is the child's father. Everyone is informed — and the child's position is abolished all the same: his entire function in the arrangement is that his face resembles another child's.

So §12 needs a supplementary criterion that does not depend on information asymmetry — and the four questions below run in that direction. (The full treatment of this case is in volume eight; here it is only a test object.)
4. What SAE Lacks Is the Carrier Layer
SAE's §7 gives a judgement at the layer of ideas; Machiavelli gives a mechanism at the layer of the carrier, and SAE does not have the latter.

§7 says war can be promoted from means to end. That is a diagnosis at the layer of ideas: the warring party has come, in the course of things, to take a means for an end. Its subject is the warring party, and a warring party is a thing that holds ideas. What Machiavelli gives is not an idea: there exists a group that eats by war. That group needs no one to make a mistake in their ideas. It need only act on its own interest, and war acquires a standing impetus.

SAE really does not have this, and it is harder than a judgement at the layer of ideas, for two reasons. It can be observed from outside. How many people in a society have their livelihood tied to a state of war is countable — the size of the standing army, employment in the arms industry, regional economies dependent on military orders. A slide in ideas cannot be counted; a tie of livelihood can. And it does not vary with intent. A wholly sincere decision-maker with no expansionist ambition still faces Machiavelli's trilemma: the men he keeps — what becomes of them when peace comes. The dilemma does not dissolve because his heart is good.

One verified point makes the judgement harder still: all six of Machiavelli's reasons are about incentive structure and social position; not one is a reason of efficiency. This series had earlier supposed the restriction's force came from holding up against efficiency — that was wrong, and the correction makes the argument stronger. If the force came from holding up against efficiency, it would be the result of a trade-off and would vary with the efficiency parameters. Coming from a diagnosis at the carrier layer, it does not vary with them.

Two consequences follow from taking it up. §7 acquires a checkable indicator: the share of the population whose livelihood is tied to a state of war. And the list of non-transferable techniques gains a cell: a technique whose operation requires establishing a professional body that lives by it carries that structural consequence with it, whatever the user's intent.
5. Arendt: Nearest in Reason, Differing on Cannot-Not
Arendt's is the closest to SAE in its reason, and the difference is that she does not handle cannot-not.

She defines power as the capacity to act in concert, and that corresponds closely to the structure of cultivation: a community's strength comes from its members' capacity to act together, not from how much coercion it can apply. SAE's §11 says nearly the same thing — the more deeply cultivated subject probably prevails, because cultivation is exactly the source of that capacity.

Where it differs: her analysis stops at violence cannot create power. The sentence is true, and it does not answer what to do when the other side is in the act of destroying your capacity to act in concert. So this is not a piece taken over to fill a gap. It is confirmation that two paths arrived at the same place, and then SAE walked on a stretch further. Theorem One handles exactly that position.
6. The Dichotomy Stands; the Derived Diagnosis Cannot Transfer Directly

Arendt's conceptual distinction between violence and power can be kept. What cannot be moved directly onto the side of the suppressed is the empirical diagnosis derived from it — that the appearance of violence proves an absence of common power. The registration has to be exact: her dichotomy fails on the side of the suppressed is too strong. What needs adjusting is not the dichotomy but a missing step of mediation when the derived diagnosis is transferred.

Her dichotomy: violence is instrumental, needs an external purpose to justify it, grows in efficacy with the improvement of the instrument; power is the capacity to act in concert, belongs to a group, and exists only while the group holds together. The derived diagnosis: to resort to violence is to prove that the capacity to act in concert no longer suffices. That diagnosis is accurate in her own domain — her book handles the relation between a regime and its own people, and a regime that turns violence inward really does show that it cannot sustain itself by concerted action.

Move it to the side of the suppressed and a step is missing. A community whose carrier of cultivation is being destroyed takes up arms not because its capacity to act in concert is insufficient — precisely because that capacity is still there, and is being cleared away by an outside force. The mediation to be supplied is a distinction: violence that replaces concerted action, appearing where concerted action can no longer be sustained, as its substitute; and violence sustained by concerted action, which is itself one form of concerted action, whose organization, mobilization and continuance all depend on that capacity.

With that distinction the dichotomy is not only kept but sharpened: in the second case violence has not become power — power is still that capacity to act in concert, and violence is one form it takes. The dichotomy is unbroken. What SAE keeps is the place of the second case, and Theorem One guards it. And this is not pointing out an error of hers. She did not draw the distinction because that was not her problem: her domain contains no such class as the organized resistance of the suppressed.
7. Kant Pushed His to the Position of a Criterion
What Kant gives in 1795 and in 1797 are two cross-sections of one thing, and the 1797 one is already a criterion rather than a diagnosis.

1795, the sixth article's sixth reason: the corruption of deceit spills over into the state of peace and destroys the purpose of peace itself. That is a diagnosis — a description of something that will happen. 1797, Doctrine of Right §57: a state under attack may use any means of defence except those that would make its subjects unfit to be citizens, because then it would itself no longer qualify to exist as a person under international law in the relations of states; and the list of prohibitions opens with using one's own subjects as spies. That is already a criterion: it lays down a prohibition and gives the anchor for judging it — the civic standing of one's own subjects.

Put together with §12, the complete shape is three segments, not two. During the war (§12): to hold an information asymmetry you must keep your own people in the dark. The criterion (§57): whether a means may be used turns on whether it makes your own subjects unfit to be citizens. After the war (1795, reason six): that way of doing things will not vanish at the armistice; it is already how this community does things.

The middle segment is what SAE lacks. SAE has the wartime diagnosis and a general judgement about cultivation, and it has never written the standing of one's own executors into an independent criterion on means. Kant did.
8. One Ground Conflict, Registered Only

Chapter five of The Prince handles cities that have lived under their own laws in freedom. He considers three courses — destroy it, go and live there, or let it keep its laws under a friendly oligarchy — and concludes: whoever becomes master of a city accustomed to freedom, and does not destroy it, may expect to be destroyed by it; for in rebellion it always has the name of liberty and its ancient privileges to fall back on, which neither time nor benefits will ever cause it to forget. He tried three roads and admits the other two are not secure.

The point of contact is clear: what destroy targets is exactly a community's capacity to reorganize itself, and that is what the bridge clause on means guards — the very thing the criterion of the last section protects. The registration is ground conflict, not internal failure and not one disagreement. By this series' discipline, what touches the ground must be criticized, and where the ground is touched one says so plainly rather than going around; writing it as a place of disagreement would misname it.

This volume registers and does not unfold it, and the reasons have to be written down. This volume's object is the user's side — the whole piece handles how a means reworks the hand that holds it, and all four mechanisms and all four questions point at the user himself. Chapter five's problem is on the other side: what it abolishes is the conquered party's capacity to reorganize, not anything of the conqueror's. That exceeds this volume's object. The unfolding is elsewhere — volume two handles it completely, including where the contact falls (he takes holding as a premise needing no argument) and the limit on it (this is not to say he is cruel). And it must not be called an internal failure here: within the problem Machiavelli set himself — how to hold a newly conquered free city — his answer is self-consistent. The trouble is in that problem's premise, and a conflict of premises is a ground conflict, not a logical failure.
9. The List of Non-Transferable Techniques

SAE has a list no one has ever drawn up: the list of non-transferable techniques — which military techniques carry structural consequences with them, such that using one means you are no longer a 15DD party.

The list can issue a verdict on one side only, and that has to be written down first. Anything that trips a screening item can be judged as carrying a structural consequence. Anything that passes them all can only be recorded as this round of screening found none of the listed structural consequences — which is not a general certificate that a 15DD party may adopt it. Writing which techniques a 15DD party may take would exceed the strength of the screening: a finite screen cannot issue a certificate; it can only record that nothing was found.

§12 gave the first cell — deceit — and by the correction above that criterion covers too little: it governs only means that depend on information asymmetry. The four mechanisms side by side give four angles of check, and together they compose the list's criterion; SAE alone cannot give it.
10. A Gate on the Ground, Before the Four Questions

Why the gate is necessary has to be said first. If the order runs all four questions passed → declare structurally neutral, then the substitution case above is let through — it passes all four and the child's position is abolished all the same. That is the shape of should have been criticized and was not: the screen for blowback on the user's side finishes, neutrality is declared, and a ground conflict was never within that screen's range at all.
The gate on the ground, before the four questions: does this arrangement abolish any particular person's independent position as an end, or use him merely as a replaceable means?

Five trigger questions go with it; any one of them hit means a candidate ground conflict is registered first, and only then may one explain why it is not one. Does it fold a particular person into the overall interest of a family, a state, an undertaking or a community? Does it abolish his independent position to refuse, to withdraw, to revise, to answer, or to reorganize himself? Is he used merely as a means — that is, does his own standing as an end fail to enter consideration in this arrangement? (Replaceability is an external indicator of this one, not its definition: an irreplaceable person can equally be used merely as a means.) Is authorisation to abolish his position as a subject obtained from an external purpose? Is consent, willingness, honour, duty or community membership treated as an automatic exemption from the prohibition on merely as a means?

The division of labour between the two gates has to be written down: the gate on the ground asks what this arrangement did to a particular person; the four questions ask what this means did to the party using it. Their objects differ, so neither can replace the other — and taking the four questions for a complete criterion is exactly that mistake.

Run the substitution case through it. It passes all four questions — no information asymmetry, no professional body, no violence, no habit formed — and it trips the gate's first, third and fifth: the child is folded into the family's overall interest; his own standing as an end does not enter consideration, his entire function being that his face resembles another child's; and willing, of his own accord is treated as an exemption from the prohibition on merely as a means. Add the gate, and that case is stopped on the spot.
11. The Four Questions
Having passed the gate, the technique enters the four screens for blowback on the user's side.

The verdict has to match the strength of the screen, and no universal may be issued here. Fail any one: this technique carries a structural consequence — that side admits a verdict, and one hit establishes it. Pass them all: one may only say on the dimensions covered by the gate and the four questions, no structural consequence was found. One may not say it is structurally neutral. The reason is this section's own: the gate's five triggers and the four screens are both non-exhaustive — the five were generalized from three known failures to criticize, and they will not stop a new one of a different shape. Two non-exhaustive screens both passed cannot support an unqualified verdict.

The questionSourceDoes this technique require one's own executors to be uninformed?SAE §12Does it require establishing a professional body that lives by it?MachiavelliWill its way of doing things still be this community's way of doing things after the armistice?KantIs it replacing concerted action rather than growing out of it?Arendt
12. Three Examples
These examples are only for testing whether the criterion is usable. They are not complete assessments of any technique — that would take knowledge at the execution layer.

Wartime secrecy — the first question asks about depth. Secrecy to the point where the executor cannot judge what he is doing: fails. Secrecy that merely withholds times and places from outsiders: passes. This cell could not be judged before; with the four questions it can, because the first question breaks the vague word secrecy into a specific question about the executor.

Total mobilization — one may not judge the second question failed. Total mobilization does not automatically establish a professional body that lives by war: a general mobilization can be temporary civic participation, disbanded when the war ends, and that is precisely the citizen army Machiavelli recommends rather than the professional soldiery he opposes. Whether the second question is hit depends on whether that mobilization produced a standing body with nowhere to go afterwards — which must be checked case by case, and cannot be settled by the phrase total mobilization. And the fourth question cannot be settled by conscript or volunteer either: conscripted means replacing concerted action, volunteered means growing out of it does not hold — a voluntary private force can equally displace public power, and a conscription can equally issue from a legitimate common decision. The fourth question asks where this technique's efficacy comes from, not how the participants enlisted.

Cognitive warfare — the third question is triggered, and triggering is not a verdict. The capacity for information manipulation it builds still exists after the war, and the capacity exists proves only that the risk exists, not that the practice must continue. Kant's reason — that vices once encouraged cannot in the nature of things be rooted out — is his claim; this volume cites it as the question's source and does not use it to declare the technique must fail.
13. One Limit, and That Fifth Question

The four questions are not exhaustive. The substitution case — everyone informed, no information asymmetry, no professional body, no violence, and no habit formed — passes all four, and that child's position was abolished all the same. So the criterion's existing four questions cannot govern this class, and the gate on the ground was set for exactly that. The relation has to be written down: this gap was found first, and the gate was added afterwards. The section stands unedited because it is the evidence for why the gate is necessary; the gap itself now has a treatment.

But one may not go a step further and say that one needs the second formula itself to appear, not these four derived checks of it — that sentence is refuted by this volume's own candidate. The candidate is: change the criterion from is the executor informed to is the executor in a position to refuse. It stops that case: the child grew up under the leverage of shame — Nitobe himself records that people will laugh at you and aren't you ashamed were the last appeal used to correct a child at fault — he is not in a position to refuse.

And what the candidate is not must be written down at once, because it very easily impersonates the gate. Able to refuse is not a complete substitute for merely as a means. A man able to refuse and not refusing may still be used merely as a means in an arrangement — consent does not change his position in it. Willing cannot make a person a means and no longer an end: the second formula does not say a person may not be used as a means without consent, it says a person may not be used merely as a means. Consent changes one aspect of the matter; it does not change that person's position in that arrangement. So the candidate can only be a fifth derived check alongside the four, never a replacement for the gate. The gate asks whether this arrangement uses him merely as a means; the fifth question asks whether he has a position from which to refuse — the latter is a common indicator of the former, not its definition.
14. Insight Is Not Enough to Make a Man Stop
The insight that a means will rebound on its user is not enough to make the man who holds it stop.

The evidence is in one and the same book. In The Art of War Machiavelli gives one of the fullest versions of this mechanism — six reasons, from livelihood to incentive to constitutional trilemma, written out layer by layer. And in chapter five of The Prince he argues for destroying a city accustomed to freedom. The two do not contradict, because they answer different questions: the first asks how a republic should arrange its internal affairs, the second how to hold a newly conquered city. He is self-consistent in both.

And that is the content of the proposition. Insight tells you what will happen; a criterion tells you what you may not do. Between them lies a stretch of road, and that stretch is walked on the ground, not on the depth of the insight. A man who sees a mechanism perfectly clearly can do, in another domain of problems, the very thing that mechanism forbids — so long as that domain has no criterion joining the two places.
This is a limit on the four-question criterion itself: it can tell a user whether a technique carries a structural consequence. It cannot make the user care about that consequence.
15. Left Unresolved in This Volume

§12's criterion is bound to the single variable of information asymmetry, and the substitution case is a counter-example — everyone informed, position abolished. Whether §12 needs a supplementary criterion independent of information asymmetry is undecided. The candidate — a fifth derived check beyond the four, is the executor in a position to refuse — already has a concrete test object, and it stops that case. Its standing must be written down: it is a derived check, not a substitute for the gate on the ground. A man able to refuse and not refusing may still be used merely as a means, so the gate can under no circumstances be replaced by it.

What remains undecided is that able to refuse is harder to verify than informed. The ownership of that difficulty is settled elsewhere: whether this criterion can be broken into publicly arguable sub-propositions is a formal question about criteria and stays inside this series; whether it can be broken apart in wartime is executive judgement and lies outside it.
And SAE lacks the middle segment — the standing of one's own executors written into an independent criterion on means. Whether to supply it on Kant's model has not been discussed.
