en/if04.title: Four Permissions
en/if04.deck: Laozi, the Sima Fa, the Mozi and SAE all refuse to treat war as an ordinary policy option — and their four gates are of four different kinds: attitude, purpose, norm, structure. The four do not all share the condition that every other road is exhausted.
units: Abstract

The Laozi, the Sima Fa, the Mozi and SAE overlap at one place: all four refuse to treat war as an ordinary policy option, and each sets up a condition of permission — by attitude, by purpose, by norm, by structure.

A stronger reading has to be ruled out at once. The four do not share a last-resort condition. The Sima Fa's to stop war by war, then war is permissible is a condition of justification; the Mozi's division between attack and chastisement is a condition of standing. Neither is a last-resort condition. Of the four, only Laozi and SAE hold one explicitly.

Four kinds of reason mark out different ranges. An attitude-type reason can lead to not fighting at all; a structural one cannot. A purpose-type reason supplies war with a legitimate result still to be attained, and therefore structurally permits widening the war for the sake of that result. A norm-type reason depends on a position that can adjudicate what is right.

And the Mohists defending cities give Theorem One's second face a real test — one this volume adjudicates. They also constitute a counter-example to a universal proposition of volume six, and force it to be rewritten.
1. How Thick the Overlap Is, and What It Is Not

Laozi 31: weapons are instruments of ill omen, not the instruments of a gentleman; he uses them only when he cannot do otherwise, and holds calm restraint the highest. Chapter 30 runs the same way: he who assists a ruler with the Way does not coerce the world with arms — such affairs are apt to rebound. The Sima Fa, Renben: so if killing men brings peace to men, killing is permissible; if attacking a state is out of love for its people, attacking is permissible; if war stops war, then even war is permissible. The Mozi, Against Offensive Warfare III, answering the challenge that Yu campaigned against the Miao, Tang against Jie, and King Wu against Zhou, and all three came to be recognised as sage kings: you have not examined the class of my words, nor understood their reason. Those were not what is called attack; they are called chastisement. And SAE's Theorem One: cannot-not — the carrier of cultivation is breached, and cultivation in a gentler form can no longer continue.

All four refuse to treat war as an ordinary policy option, and they build their respective conditions of permission out of attitude, purpose, norm and structure. The overlap is real, and it is narrower than it looks. What the four share: none accepts advantageous, therefore permissible; all require an extra gate before war begins; and all place that gate high in their own system — Laozi in the two chapters on arms, the Sima Fa in its opening paragraph, Mozi across three whole chapters, SAE at Theorem One.

What the four do not share is the character of that gate. Reading all four as the precondition every other road is exhausted does not hold. Laozi: uses them only when he cannot do otherwise — a last-resort condition indeed. SAE: the carrier breached, the gentler form no longer possible — a last-resort condition indeed. The Sima Fa: killing that brings peace is permissible, war that stops war is permissible — this is a condition of justification. It does not ask whether other roads have been walked; it asks what this war serves. A war serving the ending of war is permitted by this reason even if other roads remain. The Mozi: those are not attack, they are chastisement — this is a condition of standing. It does not ask whether other roads have been walked; it asks which class this campaign falls into. Chastisement need not first show that the roads other than chastisement are exhausted.

So of the four, only Laozi and SAE explicitly hold a last-resort condition. And the fourfold division is precisely the device that prevents the misreading: state first that the four are of different kinds, then check what each marks out. Press them into one common point at the start and every later section will be supplying reasons for a common point that does not exist.

Type of reasonWhat the gate asksLaoziattitudeWeapons are of ill omen; used only when one cannot do otherwise — a last-resort conditionSima FapurposeWhat does this war serve — a condition of justificationMozinormWhich class does this campaign fall into, attack or chastisement — a condition of standingSAEstructureIs the carrier of cultivation breached and the gentler form no longer possible — a last-resort condition
2. The Attitude Type: Laozi, and One Exit

Laozi's cannot do otherwise hangs on a judgement about weapons themselves: they are instruments of ill omen. Fine weapons are instruments of ill omen; all things may come to detest them, so one who has the Way does not dwell with them. The form of the argument is: this thing has a bad property in itself, all things detest it, so a man of the Way does not keep company with it — and therefore using it can only be being forced with no other course. It is a judgement about the character of the object, and what follows from it is an attitude — calm restraint above all, victory not to be admired, a victory in war to be received with the rites of mourning.

An attitude-type reason can lead to not fighting at all; a structural one cannot. Laozi's leaves an exit, and he walks toward it himself: since weapons are of ill omen, the best choice is not to use them at all. Chapter 30's does not coerce the world with arms and chapter 31's one who has the Way does not dwell with them both point that way.

SAE's cannot-not closes that exit. Once the structural condition is met, not fighting is not an option — it merely transfers the cost elsewhere, and usually to the part of the population least able to bear it. The difference is not one of degree. Laozi's criterion allows a man to say I will not take part in this, and supplies him a complete reason for that choice. SAE's does not, because it asks not shall I take part but is this situation already without another form.

And there is one thing Laozi has that SAE lacks. Chapter 30: he who assists a ruler with the Way does not coerce the world with arms; such affairs are apt to rebound. This is a judgement about blowback, and where it appears is worth noting: it is in the judgement about going to war, not in the judgement about means. SAE's treatment of blowback is concentrated at the layer of means — §12 on how deceit suppresses one's own side's subjecthood, and the four mechanisms set side by side in volume three all act on means. Theorem One has no such item. It asks is it unavoidable; it does not ask how will this come back on us. The item can be taken up, and the taking has a difficulty: add will it rebound to Theorem One and Theorem One acquires a component of consequence-calculation — which is exactly what the next distinction is meant to keep it clear of. How to take it up is left open.

Victory not to be admired is a second overlap, and the reasons still differ. A victory is not beautiful, and he who finds it beautiful delights in killing men… where the slain are many, weep for them in sorrow; a victory in war is to be received with the rites of mourning. §8 agrees with the conclusion: not losing is not winning. Laozi's reason: weapons are of ill omen, so success with them is not a good thing either. SAE's reason: military outcome is one dimension and passing the principle is another; winning does not constitute legitimacy in principle. The coverage differs: by Laozi's, no victory in any war deserves admiration, because weapons are of ill omen. By SAE's, a defensive war that passes the principle is not something whose completion cannot be acknowledged — what cannot be acknowledged is the inference that victory itself constitutes legitimacy. So the two block different things: Laozi blocks the glorification of war, SAE blocks settling the principle by the outcome. One blocks widely, the other blocks one specific inference squarely.
3. The Purpose Type: the Sima Fa

So if killing men brings peace to men, killing is permissible; if attacking a state is out of love for its people, attacking is permissible; if war stops war, then even war is permissible. Three sentences of one structure: the act itself — killing, attacking, warring — is not legitimate, but if it serves a legitimate result — peace, love of the people, the ending of war — then it is permitted. This places war inside a chain of means: there is an end to be reached, war is one available means to it, and within that scope it is permitted.

A purpose-type reason supplies war with a legitimate result still to be attained, and therefore structurally permits widening the war for the sake of that result. The argument: if war's permission derives from the result it serves, then so long as that result is not yet attained, this war has not yet completed its legitimacy. Continue the war in order to stop war is coherent inside this reason — it is not an abuse of it. And this is not a consequence pressed onto the text from outside. The Sima Fa writes it out itself.
4. The Extension the Sima Fa Gives Itself

In the same chapter, on the disposition after the guilty have been chastised: on entering the territory of the guilty, do no violence to the spirits, hold no hunts, damage no earthworks, burn no houses, fell no forests, take no livestock, grain or implements. Seeing the old and the young, escort them home unharmed; even meeting the able-bodied, if they do not resist, do not treat them as enemies; if they are wounded, give them medicine and send them back. This code is real, and finer than most traditions of its era. It should not be passed over. No desecration of shrines, no hunting, no wrecking of waterworks, no burning of houses, no felling of timber, no seizing of livestock, grain or tools; the old and the young sent home; the unresisting not made enemies; the wounded treated and returned.

But the clause that follows is another matter: the guilty having been chastised, the king and the feudal lords shall set that state in order, raise up the worthy and establish the enlightened, and restore its proper offices. The Sima Fa, Renben, places just punitive war and post-war political rectification within one and the same normative architecture. That is a textual fact: one chapter, one sequence of norms — first the prohibitions governing conduct on entering enemy territory, then, immediately, the rectification of that state once the guilty have been chastised. The two are contiguous in the text.

The next step is this volume's own reading, and is marked as such. If war's permission derives from the result stopping war, then securing that result belongs to the war; and a state just chastised will generate fresh disorder if its internal order is not rebuilt — so on this reason rebuilding is entailed. The text does not assert that inference. The Sima Fa nowhere says because the purpose is to stop war, political rectification is necessary; it merely places the two together. That the juxtaposition has a structural reason is this volume's holding — interpretation, not quotation. And a note on the state of the text: the five surviving chapters are the remnant of a larger ancient corpus, formed principally in the scholarly milieu of Warring States Qi while preserving an earlier stratum of military ritual, so one should not draw a strong claim about authorial logic from two propositions sharing a chapter.

But even taking only the layer of textual fact, the contrast with SAE stands. §18 prohibits precisely the act of setting that state in order, raising up the worthy and establishing the enlightened — and the Sima Fa writes it into the sequence of norms for a just war. Two normative systems giving contrary provisions at one and the same place: that does not depend on any interpretation at all.
5. Where Theorem Three Stands Here, and One Cross-Tradition Correspondence

Theorem Three requires that war be directed toward ending. But ending is not the same as attaining a legitimate result. The content of ending is: domination broken, and the possibility restored for the other party to organise itself. It does not include making the result. A situation in which domination has been broken and the other party then falls into disorder is, by Theorem Three, ended; by the Sima Fa, incomplete.

The difference can be stated precisely. The Sima Fa's terminus lies in the state of affairs — is that country now settled. SAE's lies in the relation — has the domination been broken, has the other party recovered the position from which it decides for itself. A state of affairs can be produced by the victor. A relation cannot.

And one correspondence across traditions. In the Doctrine of Right §60 (1797) Kant permits compelling an unjust enemy to adopt a constitution unfavourable by its nature to war — the same act. The two reasons are entirely different: Kant's runs through Recht (the character of that state's constitution is a property identifiable from outside), the Sima Fa's through the stopping of war (the result must be secured). Two wholly different paths landing at the same place shows this is not one tradition's deviation. It is the common exit of the practice of setting a legitimate goal for war — once legitimacy derives from a result to be attained, securing the result belongs to the war, and the most direct way to secure it is to build the order on the other party's behalf. (Kant's provision is treated in full in volume one of this series.)
6. The Norm Type: the Mozi, and That Adjudicating Position

The argument of Against Offensive Warfare I is an analogy. A man enters another's orchard and steals his peaches and plums, and all condemn him; killing an innocent man, stripping him of his clothes, taking his spear and sword, is more unrighteous still than taking another's horse or ox, because the injury to others is greater. In such cases the gentlemen of the world all know to condemn it. Yet when it comes to the great unrighteousness of attacking a state, they do not know to condemn it; they follow along and praise it and call it righteous. Can this be called knowing the distinction between righteous and unrighteous? The structure is clear: unrighteousness increases with the injury done — and this is an inconsistency in logic, not a divergence in values. Mozi presses it to the extreme: killing one man is called unrighteous and incurs one capital penalty; killing a hundred is a hundredfold unrighteousness and incurs a hundred capital penalties; while attacking a state kills by the ten thousand and is called righteous — seeing a little black one calls it black, seeing much black one calls it white. That is not a difference in values but an inability to tell black from white.

But in Against Offensive Warfare III, answering the challenge, Mozi introduces a division: those are not what is called attack; they are called chastisement. The division is clean, and it places the whole weight on one thing: who adjudicates whether this is attack or chastisement. Mozi's criterion is to promote what benefits the world and eliminate what harms it — a substantive standard requiring someone to certify it. And the instances he cites for the three sage kings all appeal to the mandate of Heaven: the Miao were in great disorder and Heaven decreed their destruction; Xia's virtue was in great disorder and Heaven then commanded Tang. In his setting the adjudicator is Heaven, and Heaven's will is displayed through portents — a sun-prodigy at night, three days of blood-rain, a dragon born in the temple, a red bird bearing a jade tablet.

A norm-type reason depends on a position from which what is right can be adjudicated. This is isomorphic with just war theory, which likewise requires a position from which to determine who the just party is — and among states no adjudicator acknowledged by all parties exists. That structure is treated in full in volume five; two points only are recorded here. First, SAE does not establish that position. Theorem One does not ask whether this war is attack or chastisement; it asks after structural conditions verifiable from outside.

Second, what Mozi has and SAE does not must be acknowledged. The analogical argument of Against Offensive Warfare I does not depend on the mandate of Heaven — it is a pure consistency argument, and anyone who grants that greater injury is greater unrighteousness must accept its conclusion. Its force is independent of the adjudicating position, and it engages precisely the class of opponent SAE finds hardest: one who justifies aggression by saying his side is righteous. Mozi's method is not to argue about righteousness with him, but to point out that his measure differs between small matters and large. SAE can use this, and SAE currently has no equally forceful form of it.
7. Bude-yi and Bude-bu

Bude-yi — having no alternative — is a judgement about the agent's situation. Bude-bu — cannot-not — requires structural conditions verifiable from outside. Of the four, Laozi comes closest, since bude-yi does structurally point at there is no other way rather than at unwillingly. But the centres of gravity differ. Bude-yi centres on the agent — he was forced to it, he had no other choice, he did it and took no pleasure in it; Laozi's calm restraint above all and victory not to be admired say exactly this. Bude-bu centres on the situation — whether those forms are still open, irrespective of what the agent wants or feels.

And so bude-yi can be sincerely mistaken; bude-bu cannot. A man can sincerely feel he has no alternative. Fear, humiliation, misinformation, incomplete knowledge can all produce that feeling, and produce it without a trace of insincerity. Laozi's criterion has no guard against this, because it was never about the structure of a situation. And in this matter, being sincerely mistaken is as fatal as being insincere. This is SAE's practical reason for putting the criterion in structure rather than in attitude — not that structure is finer than attitude, but that a feeling cannot be reviewed, and the cost of war is not borne by feelings.

One cost must be acknowledged at once. Whether a structural condition can be verified is itself a question: whether cultivation in its gentler form can still continue cannot be counted the way one's own casualties can be counted. So the difference stated above is a difference in principle — an attitude-type criterion is unverifiable in principle, while a structural one is verifiable in principle and not always in practice. The difference is real, and it is smaller than it looks.
8. The Mohists Defending Cities: the Material

The Mohists did not merely oppose offensive war; they organised armed parties to help other states hold their walls. This is the only material in pre-Qin China that can be brought to bear on the second face of Theorem One. Gongshu: Gongshu Ban had built scaling ladders for Chu, to attack Song; Mozi set out from Qi and walked ten days and ten nights to Ying, and persuaded first Gongshu Ban, then the king. The king conceded the argument: well said — even so, Gongshu Ban has made me scaling ladders; I must take Song. The argument did not stop the war.

There followed the simulated siege: Mozi unfastened his belt to make a wall and used slips of wood for engines; Gongshu Ban deployed nine changes of siege machinery and Mozi repelled all nine — Gongshu Ban's engines were exhausted and Mozi's defence had margin to spare. Gongshu Ban said he knew how to defeat him but would not say it; Mozi said he knew it too, and would not say it either. Asked the meaning, Mozi answered: Gongshu's intent is nothing more than to kill me. Kill me, and Song will be unable to hold and can be attacked. But three hundred of my disciples, including Qin Huali, already hold my defensive implements upon the walls of Song, awaiting the invaders from Chu. Though you kill me, you cannot cut them off.

Preparing the City Gates opens with Qin Huali asking how a small state may be defended, and Mozi's answer is not about equipment: our walls and moats repaired, defensive implements ready, firewood and grain sufficient, superiors and inferiors in mutual affection, and further the aid of the neighbouring lords — by these one holds. And though the defender be skilled, if the ruler does not employ him, still one cannot hold… therefore the defender must be skilled and the ruler must honour and employ him; only then can one hold. The second passage lists fourteen conditions for holding a city, and its conclusion is very strong: where not one of the fourteen is present, then even a skilled man cannot hold it.
9. Isomorphic with §11, and the Ruler Honouring and Employing Him

Preparing the City Gates makes the condition of subjects within the community a necessary condition of a city's defensibility, isomorphic with §11 of the treatise. Of the fourteen, walls, moats, towers, implements, grain and terrain are material conditions; while officials and people in accord, the ruler trustworthy and just and the myriad people delighting in him without end, the graves of fathers and mothers are there, deep resentment against the enemy and great merit toward one's superiors, rewards clear and credible and punishments severe enough to be feared — these are conditions internal to the community. This is deepening cultivation is national strength in Warring States form — whether a community can hold itself depends on its internal condition, not on how good a technician it has hired.

And the defender must be skilled and the ruler must honour and employ him; only then can one hold corresponds to the genuine rising gate on the second face of Theorem One. The force of the sentence lies in its negative form: however good the defender, if the ruler does not employ him, the city still cannot be held. Mozi is not discussing courtesy; he is stating an operational fact — the party being defended must itself want to defend. And the practice recorded in Gongshu matches: Mozi went first to dissuade the attacker while sending disciples to assist Song's defence, not to take it over. Nowhere in the chapter does he demand that Song hand over command, and nowhere does he establish anything in Song.
10. The Gate of the Intervening Party's Own Interests: a Determination

Among the four gates on the second face of Theorem One, the hardest is that an intervening party must have interests of its own — the gate exists to prevent deciding on others' behalf whether they should resist. What were the Mohists' own interests? They were not men of Song. Gongshu adds one detail at its close: Mozi returned, and passing through Song it rained; he took shelter in a gateway, and the gatekeeper would not let him in. The state he had saved did not know him, and would not let him in out of the rain. That detail rules out any motive of reward.

The Mohists' defence of cities satisfies the gate, but their interest lies at the level of a community's continued existence, not at the level of benefit. Mohism was a community with a definite doctrine, a definite organisation, a definite way of life; and that community's continuation required one condition — that there exist a number of independent small states, some of whose rulers were willing to listen and to employ them. In a world annexed to the end, that condition disappears. Mozi calculated this himself in Against Offensive Warfare II: of the states enfeoffed in antiquity, those destroyed by offensive war are beyond counting; Ju in the east was a very small state, wedged between Qi and Yue, and in the end perished. In a world where the small states have all been swallowed, Mohism has nowhere to go. So stopping attacks is not altruism; it is guarding one's own carrier — only that carrier is not property or territory but a world in which small states still exist and someone is still willing to hear a doctrine.

The consequence of this determination is that the sense of the gate is broader than first supposed: it does not require the intervening party to have material gains or losses at stake, only that the intervening party's carrier of cultivation genuinely depends on the outcome of the intervention. The contrary possibility must be stated. Read more strictly — requiring a direct, identifiable common interest between intervening and intervened — the Mohists do not satisfy it, and Theorem One would then determine that the practice closest to 15DD in pre-Qin China fails its criterion. This volume adopts the broad reading, on the ground that the strict reading would exclude all cross-community assistance, which is not what this gate exists to prevent. What it exists to prevent is deciding on others' behalf whether they should resist — and the Mohists left precisely that decision to the other side.
11. Stopping War in Gongshu Is Not Attacking the Plan

Sunzi's attacking the enemy's plans is destroying the other side's design so that it cannot stand. In Gongshu the king's plan was not destroyed: having conceded the argument he still said I must take Song. What changed the outcome were two things — the result of the simulated siege, nine attacks repelled nine times; and the fact that three hundred men were already on Song's walls with defensive implements. This is making the attack fail on cost, not making the plan fail.

And its precondition is that the defence was already in place. Had Qin Huali's three hundred not been on Song's walls, neither the advocacy nor the sand-table exercise would have stopped the king — Mozi says so plainly: kill me, and Song cannot hold, and can be attacked. This is a historical specimen of §10's not fighting is also preparing, and the specimen gives a more specific form: preparation is part of what makes attacking-the-plan work, not the next step after it has failed. Sunzi's four-rung sequence — attack the plan, attack alliances, attack the army, attack cities — implies a temporal order; in Gongshu, preparation and persuasion proceed simultaneously, and preparation is the condition of persuasion working at all.

This bears directly on Theorem One's threshold. If preparation is the condition of attacking-the-plan working, then attacking-the-plan exhausted cannot be understood as saying everything one can say while unprepared. And this is a concrete instance of a more general dependency: determining whether that threshold is satisfied requires knowing what options attacking-the-plan and attacking-alliances comprise and under what conditions each works — which is execution-layer knowledge, and SAE explicitly does not do the execution layer. A layer of principle may declare that it does not do the execution layer. It may not declare that it does not depend on one. The full treatment is in volume six.
12. Mohism as a Counter-Example, and the Rewriting

The proposition tested here comes from volume six, and is stated in full because everything in this section depends on it. Original form, universal: constraints on the enemy-facing side can be generated by reciprocal equilibrium — one does not strike a state in mourning, does not exploit a natural disaster, drums only once the enemy has formed his ranks; such rules arise and persist because the other side observes them too, and a violator meets the same treatment next time. Whereas on one's own side there is no counterparty to enforce. Who redeems the soldier's standing to be informed? Who makes a commander pay for violating it? In a one-directional structure where reward, punishment, life and death all issue from the commander, no mechanism can stabilise such a constraint — such constraints therefore lack the conditions of their generation. That proposition flagged Mohism as a possible counter-example, because the Mohists were a transnational organisation whose internal discipline was enforced by no state's military law.

Mohism is a counter-example to the original universal form, and forces the rewriting of its domain and its table of mechanisms. To say Mohism is not a counter-example, only an addition does not hold: if the original proposition is universal — no generative mechanism on one's own side — then a single sample with a non-reciprocal constraint on that side is a counter-example. Lu's Questions records that Mozi sent his disciple Sheng Chuo to serve Xiangzi Niu; Xiangzi Niu invaded Lu three times and Sheng Chuo followed him three times. Hearing of it, Mozi sent Gao Sunzi to request his withdrawal — he recalled his own student. His reason: to speak of righteousness and not act on it is knowingly to transgress. It is not that Chuo did not know; his salary outweighed his righteousness. This is a discipline on a member of one's own side, and its support is not reciprocity: Sheng Chuo could not punish Mozi, and Mozi had nothing to fear from him.

But its support is not humanity is an end either — this distinction is the easiest thing in the section to misread. What stabilised Mohist discipline was a bundle of institutional conditions, not the standing of a norm on its own: rules acknowledged as constitutive of the community (not to keep them is not to be a Mohist); an internal authority and review mechanism (the office of the Grand Master); real consequences for violation (recall, expulsion); exit a real and not merely nominal possibility (voluntary entry, and one may leave); a channel for appeal and reinterpretation (the Mohist tradition of disputation). The character of this bundle must be stated: these five are candidate conditions generalised from a single sample, untested for necessity or sufficiency, and Mohism has all five is itself overstated — the Grand Master and expulsion have textual support, rules acknowledged as constitutive is supported by to speak of righteousness and not act on it is knowingly to transgress, while the channel of appeal comes from a general impression of the Mohist tradition of disputation, for which this volume has no specific citation.

And a distinction must be carried through: why a norm holds and how a norm comes to be stably enforced within an organisation are two things. Humanity is an end does not fail because institutions are inadequate — in a community without a Grand Master, treating a person merely as a means is still not legitimate. And that the office of Grand Master could stabilise discipline does not show that the discipline was legitimate. So what this section gives is a hypothesis about institutional stability, not a judgement about the source of norms.

The rewritten form: self-limitations on the enemy-facing side can be stabilised by reciprocity; self-limitations on one's own side cannot depend on the other party's retaliation, and must be stabilised otherwise — by internal rights, procedures, membership structures, or institutional review. Reciprocity is not the only mechanism by which constraints are generated. This form has a real boundary of application: Mohists could leave Mohism; soldiers cannot leave an army. All five conditions fail in a conscript army — membership is not voluntary, the cost of exit is death, there is no internal review, there is no channel of appeal. So after the revision, a conscripted army still falls on the side of the conditions of generation are absent. And the corollary attached to the original proposition is unaffected: a constraint hung on reciprocity is effective only on the face where reciprocity obtains, while a criterion hung on humanity is an end takes effect without requiring the other party to be capable of retaliation. That is the practical reason for placing a criterion on the ground rather than on custom — custom disappears where reciprocity disappears, and on one's own side there was never any reciprocity to be had.
13. Left Unresolved in This Volume

Laozi's such affairs are apt to rebound is a blowback mechanism situated in the judgement about going to war, and Theorem One has no counterpart — SAE's blowback mechanisms all sit at the layer of means. Whether to take it up is undecided, and the difficulty is that taking it up would add a component of consequence-calculation to Theorem One, which the distinction between bude-yi and bude-bu exists precisely to keep it clear of.

The broad reading of the own-interests gate has an undetermined boundary: what counts as depending on? Does a community that merely cares, in thought, about another's fate satisfy it? This volume does not answer. And that preparation is a condition of attacking-the-plan working deepens Theorem One's threshold into a dependency on execution-layer knowledge, treated in volume six.

Finally: the consistency argument of Against Offensive Warfare I — seeing a little black one calls it black, seeing much black one calls it white — engages the class of opponent who justifies aggression by claiming righteousness more directly than any form SAE currently has. Whether SAE should adopt an argument of the same type has not been considered.
14. A Note on the Title

This volume, like the rest of the series, keeps its correction records in the body: withdrawn propositions, narrowed claims and downgraded conclusions are marked where they occurred rather than silently repaired. They are kept for a reason — a framework that requires the claim cannot-not to be questioned must itself be the first thing questioned, and a text that shows no sign of ever having erred gives its reader no way to judge how its determinations were reached.

In this volume the point bears on the title itself. A title such as Four Ways of Having Nowhere Left to Go would presuppose that all four traditions share a last-resort condition — and the first section shows they do not. What a volume is called must answer to what it can establish.

en/if05.title: That Position Is Left Empty
en/if05.deck: The four theorems are most easily read as a new just war theory. This volume exists to prevent that misreading: SAE does not establish the position from which to determine who is the just party — and Grotius stands on the same side.
units: Abstract
This volume exists to prevent a misreading. SAE's four theorems are most easily read as a new just war theory — determine who is the just party, and go to war and punish on that basis.

The overlap with the just war tradition is real, in three groups: a high threshold for going to war; means not exempted by the justice of the end; and war directed toward the restoration of peace. Three reasons differ, and the differences in range can be named one by one. Last resort as a moral duty can be offset by exigency; as a structural condition it cannot. Proportionality and SAE's bridge clause on means intersect rather than contain one another. Rousseau's principle of discrimination depends on both parties to a war being states, and fails in non-state war; SAE's does not.

Two disagreements: auctoritas principis does not block the self-defence of the powerless — it prevents a private act of defence from automatically carrying the juridical powers of public war. And supreme emergency permits cancelling the other party's carrier of cultivation to preserve one's own; SAE declines that permission and bears the cost of declining. This is registered as a ground conflict, not as internal failure.

One structural divergence: applying these criteria in full requires a position from which to determine who is the just party, and among states no such position exists. Grotius faced that absence squarely, and SAE stands on the same side as he does — both decline to establish the position and turn instead to governing conduct in its absence. The cost of leaving it empty is that SAE issues no certificate of legitimacy usable to persuade a third party.
1. The Overlap, in Three Groups

The overlap is stated in full first; otherwise what follows will read as fault-finding, and the likeliest error in this volume is to state the overlap too thinly. The tradition's jus ad bellum requires just cause, right authority, right intention, last resort, reasonable hope of success and proportionality; SAE's Theorem One requires that the carrier of cultivation be lost, that cultivation in its mild forms can no longer continue, and that four gates be passed. Both hold that beginning a war requires a high threshold, and both place have the other roads been walked among the hardest of the conditions.

Jus in bello has two core principles: discrimination — non-combatants may not be made the direct object of attack — and proportionality. SAE has the bridge clause constraining means: no means may be used that forecloses the other party's possibility of reorganising itself as a subject of cultivation. Both hold that means acquire no exemption from the justice of the end. This is no small matter: it means both systems reject the end justifies the means, and in the domain of war that rejection is not self-evident. And the tradition requires right intention — the aim is the restoration of peace, not conquest, revenge or plunder — while SAE's Theorem Three requires that war be directed toward ending.

And one sentence must be added, not as argument but as fact. From Augustine through Aquinas to Grotius, this line drew war out of the strong may do anything and put it inside a set of criteria that could be publicly argued, cited, and used to indict rulers. Modern law of war grew from it. Every divergence in this volume proceeds on that premise.

GroupThe traditionSAEThreshold for warJust cause, right authority, right intention, last resort, hope of success, proportionalityTheorem One: the carrier lost, mild forms exhausted, four gates passedLimits on meansDiscrimination and proportionalityThe bridge clause: no means may foreclose the other party's reorganisationDirectionRight intention — the restoration of peaceTheorem Three: directed toward ending
2. Last Resort: a Moral Duty and a Structural Condition

The tradition's is a moral duty: you are obliged to try peaceful means first, and a ruler who goes to war without trying, even with just cause, is morally at fault. SAE's is a structural condition: cultivation in its mild forms can no longer continue. That is not a duty but a judgement about a situation — whether those forms are still open.

A last resort of the duty type can be offset by exigency; one of the structural-condition type cannot. In moral reasoning the stringency of a duty is generally modulated by circumstance: I ought to have negotiated first, but they were already massing; there was no time is an available defence, and often an accepted one. Requirements adjusting to feasibility is not a flaw in moral reasoning — it is how it normally works. A structural condition admits no such adjustment. Urgency does not change whether those roads are still open. If the road of negotiation remains open and was not walked, Theorem One's condition is not met, however pressed the agent.

One practical consequence: at the moment when error is likeliest — the other side massing, reports confused, the window for decision narrowing — the binding force of a duty-type criterion is at its weakest, because that is exactly when circumstances did not permit is most persuasive. The criterion is loosest when it is most needed.

But one cost must be acknowledged. A condition wholly unmodulated by circumstance may in practice appear inhuman, and may require an agent to walk through a procedure that has become meaningless when he knows the other side is about to strike. SAE's only answer is that the condition asks not was the procedure completed but is that road still open — and a road the other party has closed does not count as open. But that answer pushes the burden of judgement back onto the agent — and the agent is in the position least fit to make it: angry, exhausted, afraid, and with good reason to think that waiting longer will kill him. These are not his faults; they are his situation. This volume does not solve that; it registers it. (The full treatment of that burden is in volume seven.)
3. Proportionality and the Bridge Clause: Intersection, Not Containment

Proportionality: the harm caused by a means may not exceed the value of the legitimate end pursued. The bridge clause: no means may foreclose the other party's possibility of reorganising itself as a subject of cultivation. The two block partly different things, and the bridge clause is not an upgrade of proportionality.

Direction one — the bridge clause blocks what proportionality does not. Proportionality is a judgement of magnitude, and it requires someone to put both sides on one scale. In war that weigher is usually the belligerent itself: it weighs the value of its own ends and the harm to the other, and every party will hold its ends to be of very high value. The bridge clause is a judgement of direction and needs no scale. It asks not how heavy was this blow but is that road still there afterwards. A belligerent may sincerely hold its end to be of infinite value; it cannot sincerely hold that a means which forecloses the other's possibility of reorganisation has not foreclosed it — that is a fact about the structure of consequences, not an assessment of value.

Direction two — proportionality blocks what the bridge clause does not. A military action that forecloses nothing yet is grossly disproportionate to its aim — heavy civilian casualties in taking a secondary objective, where those casualties do not destroy the other party's capacity to reorganise — draws no verdict from the bridge clause, and does draw one from proportionality. This must be stated plainly: SAE has a gap here. The bridge clause handles does it foreclose; it does not handle is it excessive. And excess is a real moral dimension, not something to be waved off with we do not make judgements of magnitude.

Direction three — the relation is intersection, not containment. So it is inaccurate to say the bridge clause is more fundamental or more thorough. They are two lines cut in different directions, and a system holding the bridge clause and not proportionality lets through an entire class of acts that ought to be blocked. Whether SAE needs an additional criterion of magnitude is not answered here — and the difficulty is that a criterion of magnitude requires a weigher, and admitting a weigher re-establishes the very position this volume declines.
4. Discrimination: the Premise of Rousseau's Version

Rousseau gives the most famous formulation, in The Social Contract I.4: war is not a relation between man and man, but between State and State, and individuals are enemies only accidentally — not as men, nor even as citizens, but as soldiers; not as members of their country, but as its defenders. And then the conclusion: since the object of war is to destroy the enemy State, it is legitimate to kill its defenders as long as they are carrying arms; but as soon as they lay them down and surrender, they cease to be enemies or instruments of the enemy, and become once more merely men, whose life no one has any right to take. The reasoning is clean, and its force comes from that premise.

Rousseau's reason is the social contract: the parties to a war are two juridical persons, and individuals stand in an adversarial relation only while serving as units of war — lay down the arms and that status ends, and with it the adversarial relation. SAE's reason is different: the other party may not be struck out of the position of a subject of cultivation, whether or not he is at this moment serving as a unit of war.

Rousseau's principle of discrimination depends on the premise that both parties to a war are states, and fails in non-state war; SAE's does not depend on that premise. Rousseau states the premise very explicitly himself: in the same passage he holds that war between private persons can exist neither in the state of nature nor in the social state; that duels and private affrays do not constitute a state of war; that the private wars of the Middle Ages were an abuse of feudalism. He expressly excludes non-state violent conflict from war. So in civil war, insurrection, non-state armed resistance and decentralised resistance, individuals are enemies only accidentally does not obtain, because there are not two juridical persons.

The consequence is not hypothetical. The 15DD defence this series is concerned with is very often of exactly that kind: resistance in occupied territory, colonial revolt, self-defence in a society whose legitimate institutions have been destroyed. A slave uprising has no juridical personality — on Rousseau's framework the principle of discrimination does not apply there, not that it is violated, but that it does not apply. SAE's does not depend on juridical statehood, because a subject of cultivation need not be a state. And what Rousseau has that SAE lacks must be acknowledged: his reasoning yields an observable moment — the moment arms are laid down, a line both sides can identify. SAE's still exists as a subject of cultivation has no such moment; it requires judgement. In actual fighting, an observable line is more useful than a more correct line that requires judgement.
5. Legitimate Authority: a Reading Corrected

The tradition requires that only legitimate public authority may make war. An earlier version of this series read that as excluding the self-defence of the powerless. That reading is too broad, and it is corrected here.

Aquinas explicitly permits private self-defence. Summa Theologiae II-II q.64 a.7: an individual may use proportionate force to preserve his own life, even where the act foreseeably results in the assailant's death — provided the defender's intention is his own preservation rather than killing, and the force is not excessive. He says the act may have two effects: the preservation of one's own life, and the death of the assailant. The line he draws is elsewhere: a private person may generally not intend the assailant's death; intentional lethal coercion belongs to public authority acting for the common good. A soldier against an enemy, an officer against a felon, may intend lethal action under public authority — and even they are at fault if acting from private enmity.

So what auctoritas principis blocks is not the self-defence of the powerless. It prevents a private act of defence from automatically carrying the juridical powers of public war — to initiate, to punish, to mobilise, to intend to kill. And Aquinas gives more than a slogan: a private person may not make war, because in a normal political condition he may assert his right before a superior's tribunal; nor can a private person summon the multitude that public war requires; conversely, the care of the common good is entrusted to public authority, which must repel enemies without as it uses public coercion against wrongdoers within. The substance of this gate is public jurisdiction, responsibility for the common good, and the prevention of a private quarrel being converted into public war.
6. SAE's Actual Distance from Him, and Where the Threshold Sits

The distance is smaller than it is usually taken to be, and that must be acknowledged. The four gates on the second face of Theorem One — do not open the second face on its own; see without substituting; genuine rising; the intervening party must have interests of its own — block the same class of things. An armed body claiming to represent the oppressed with no one having asked it fails the third gate; an intervener with no connection to the party intervened for fails the fourth; an action packaging a private quarrel as liberation fails the first. Aquinas's reasons address the same class of danger that the four gates exist to prevent. To say that SAE rejects legitimate authority and is therefore more permissive is inaccurate.

The real difference is where the threshold is set: he sets it on the standing of the subject, SAE on the structure of the situation. Standing is a judgement about who this person is — does he hold public office, whence does his authority derive. Structure is a judgement about what this situation is like — has the carrier been lost, has the other party risen, is the intervener connected.

And the difference in range runs both ways. Direction one: a collective self-defence in a society whose legitimate institutions have been destroyed cannot be raised to the status of war under auctoritas principis — it may be an indefinite number of individual acts of justified defence, but it cannot be a war with standing to be initiated, to mobilise, to punish. And 15DD defence is very often exactly that situation. SAE's four gates do not ask this; they ask after structural conditions, and those have nothing to do with holding public office.

Direction two: standing is verifiable; structure is hard to verify. Does this king have the authority to declare war could be checked at the time; is the rising genuine requires judgement. This tells against SAE, and the cost must be stated: it is another appearance of one and the same problem — a structural condition is verifiable in principle while lacking, in practice, any settled way of being observed. The attribution of that problem divides in two: can this criterion be broken into publicly contestable sub-propositions is a question about the form of a criterion, and falls within what this series must answer; can it be broken down in wartime is an execution judgement, and does not.
7. Supreme Emergency: a Ground Conflict

Walzer holds that when the threat facing a political community is extreme enough to destroy its very existence, the limits of jus in bello may be breached. This is the strongest direct challenge to the bridge clause on means, because it does not claim the clause is wrong. It claims there exists a tier of exception at which rules give way to survival.

What supreme emergency permits is: to preserve our own carrier of cultivation, the other party's may be cancelled. SAE declines that permission and bears the cost of declining. The registration must be precise. To write this does not hold within SAE would not itself be wrong — it indeed cannot be uttered within SAE — but it reads as a determination that the concept is self-contradictory, and Walzer is not inside SAE, so that determination does not apply to him. The accurate statement is: this is SAE's choice of ground, not a determination about the internal consistency of the concept. Walzer's argument is coherent within his own framework, and he advanced it in full awareness of the difficulty.

The argument: the bridge clause prohibits foreclosing the other party's possibility of reorganising itself as a subject of cultivation — and what supreme emergency asks to exempt is precisely that class of means; it exempts what is ordinarily forbidden, which is to say the most thorough. So the content of the exception is: when one party's carrier of cultivation is threatened, the other's may be cancelled. And that cannot be uttered within SAE, for a reason of the same form as volume two's: cultivation cannot authorise the cancellation of cultivation. A criterion in the name of preserving cultivation whose content is cancelling the other party's cultivation cancels the condition of its own standing. It has not violated a rule; it does not obtain.

But the cost must be acknowledged, and the acknowledgement cannot be merely formal. Walzer's exception was not set down carelessly; it answers to a real situation — there are moments at which keeping the rules may mean the destruction of a community. SAE's refusal of the exception is the bearing of that cost: it issues no exception clause available to be invoked at such a moment, and a community in that situation gets no dispensation from SAE. That bearing must be written down; the situation may not be pretended away. And what SAE bears it on must also be written: not that the situation will not arise, but that once the exception is established, any party may claim to stand at that tier, and no one has standing to verify the claim.
8. That Position

The foregoing can be discussed item by item. One thing cannot, because it determines that the two are not of one kind. The full application of these criteria requires a position from which to determine who is the just party, and among states no such position exists. Just cause, right intention, proportionality — each of these judgements must be made, and among states there exists no maker of them whom all parties acknowledge.

The position then has only these destinations: left empty, and the criteria cannot be applied; occupied by the belligerents themselves, and each judges itself just, so the criteria lose their discriminating power; or occupied by some third party claiming standing — and whence that third party's standing? Historically the position has been occupied in turn by the Church, by the sovereign state itself after Westphalia, and in our time by something called international society. All three have had real functions, and all three have had their standing questioned.
9. Grotius Faced It Squarely, and SAE Stands on His Side

An earlier version of this series wrote that the position has only three destinations, and none of them holds. That exhaustive list omits a fourth, supplied here. Grotius knew clearly that among sovereign states there is no common judge of the kind available to litigants within a civil state — that absence is the very problem his theory of war addresses, not something he failed to see. And his answer has three tiers.

First, the tier of objective natural right: contradictory claims cannot both be true in the same respect, so objectively a war cannot ordinarily be just on both sides. Second, the tier of subjective culpability: a party whose cause is objectively defective may nonetheless act from excusable or invincible error — so objectively both sides cannot be just and both sides may have justified belief in their own justice do not conflict. Third, the tier of the law of nations: the law of nations may confer bilateral legal effects on a formal public war — the validity of capture, the standing of acts in war — even where the natural justice of the original cause cannot belong to both. The third tier does the most important work: it lets every soldier and every third party know which legal consequences of the war apply without first settling the dispute over just cause. So the fourth destination of that position is: do not adjudicate; govern conduct in the unadjudicated state.

The criticism that remains live is that the response yields no authoritative third-party determination. This tradition has no answer to the question does not. And here SAE and Grotius are on the same side, which changes the shape of this volume. Both decline to establish the adjudicating position, and both turn instead to governing conduct in the unadjudicated state. The difference lies in what is governed: Grotius governs the symmetrical distribution of legal effects — both sides fall under the same rules on capture, the status of prisoners, the validity of acts in war, without asking whose cause is objectively just. SAE governs whether the standing as a subject is preserved — the bridge clause asks whether, after the fighting, the other party can reorganise itself, and likewise does not ask whose cause is objectively just. Neither regime requires an adjudicator, and both are verifiable from outside. At this point SAE is not opposed to the tradition; it has taken another road in a direction the tradition had already opened.
10. Kant: the Position Cannot Be Established

Theorem One does not ask whether this war is just. It asks: has the carrier of cultivation been lost; can cultivation in its mild forms no longer continue; have the four gates been passed. These are judgements about structure, requiring not standing but sight.

And Kant, from within Recht, holds that the position cannot be established. Perpetual Peace, Sixth Preliminary Article: war is only the sad recourse in the state of nature — where there is no tribunal which could judge with the force of law — by which each state asserts its right by violence; and in it neither party can be adjudged unjust, for that would presuppose a juridical decision; in place of that decision the issue of the conflict, as in a so-called judgment of God, decides on which side the right is. But between states no punitive war is conceivable, because there exists between them no relation of superior and inferior.

The position of this passage matters: it speaks from within Recht, not against Recht from outside. Kant does not say the moral concerns of just war theory are wrong. He says the adjudicating position does not exist among states — not ought not to be established but cannot be, because establishing it requires a juridical decision for which there is no judge, and because punishment presupposes a relation of superior and inferior which does not obtain. So SAE need not draw this distinction itself: someone on that road has already drawn it. (In the Doctrine of Right §60 of 1797 Kant employs the concept of an unjust enemy, which does not sit easily with this; that is treated in volume one.)
11. The Cost of Leaving It Empty

The cost of leaving the adjudicating position empty is that SAE issues no certificate of legitimacy usable to persuade a third party. Just war theory issues that certificate. It is one of the tradition's real functions and one reason it has been needed for two thousand years — a community deciding to resist needs to explain to its own members, to possible allies and to posterity why the thing is right. Our war is just is a sentence that can be said, quoted, and written into a declaration.

SAE's criterion produces no such sentence. What it produces is in this structure, entering war constitutes a cannot-not — a sentence meaningful only where the specific structure obtains, and acceptable only to someone willing to go and check that structure. This is not clumsiness of expression but structural necessity: once SAE issues that certificate, the adjudicating position has been re-established, because a certificate requires a signatory.

From this follows one requirement on the reader. The place where the four theorems are most easily conflated with just war theory is exactly where they most resemble it — high threshold, limits on means, peace as the aim. So it must be said flatly: the four theorems do not determine who is the just party. They tell no one you are right and he is wrong. They determine one thing: whether, in this specific structure, entering war constitutes a cannot-not, and which practices, once entered, turn the thing into something else. This determination faces inward — a criterion turned inward is reflection; turned outward it is judgement. A use of the four theorems to argue that one is oneself just, and the other unjust, has read them as a just war theory, and that is the misreading this volume exists to prevent.
12. One Asymmetry That Must Be Acknowledged

Leaving the adjudicating position empty does not exempt SAE from misuse. Anyone who wants a war can say the mild forms are exhausted, just as he can say our war is just. Both require external verification, and both are hard to verify in wartime. The difference is only this: the former can be broken into sub-propositions that can be publicly argued and separately evidenced — which roads were walked, what did the other party answer, which measures remain untried — while the latter points at a holistic judgement.

Three things must be stated precisely, because decomposability is very easily read as verifiability. First, each item after decomposition can still be disputed — whether a road was genuinely open, whether a given response constitutes closure, whether an attempt was sufficient: none of these has an automatic answer. Decomposability is not automatic transparency of fact. Second, what decomposability buys is localisation of dispute, assignable burdens of proof, locatable error, and a handle for revision — not the truth. Third, a holistic judgement cannot be refuted is also too strong: it can be opposed, there is simply nowhere for the opposition to take hold — an opponent can only deny it wholesale, and a wholesale denial is as unadjudicable as the wholesale assertion.

What survives the narrowing: SAE's criterion directs dispute toward places where it can be handled item by item, and just war theory's does not. This is an advantage of degree, not of kind. And the realisation of that advantage depends on someone actually asking — which is Theorem Four's business, and one of SAE's thinnest places.
13. Left Unresolved in This Volume

Proportionality blocks a class the bridge clause does not — foreclosing nothing, yet grossly disproportionate. Whether SAE needs an additional criterion of magnitude is undecided, and the difficulty is that a criterion of magnitude requires a weigher, while admitting a weigher re-establishes the position this volume declines. Without it, an entire class that ought to be blocked is not blocked.

Structural checks are harder to verify than checks of standing, and the attribution of that problem is handled separately. Supreme emergency is declined partly on the ground that any party may claim to stand at that tier and no one has standing to verify the claim — but the same words can be turned against SAE's own threshold, as this volume concedes. The difference is one of degree, and a difference of degree needs its size stated; this volume does not quantify it.

Finally: Rousseau's discrimination supplies an observable moment — arms laid down — while SAE's still exists as a subject of cultivation does not. Whether SAE needs an observable operational marker has not been considered.
